utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday we were unable to get an answer to the question: Which is the oldest building of Albanian architecture in Kosovo and Metohija? Can you tell us, at least roughly, what dates the oldest monuments of Albanian architecture date back to?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought I tried to answer this question last time. The Islamic architecture, as I described, goes back to the fifteenth century. There is residential architecture which one could qualify as traditional Albanian architecture that's a couple of centuries younger. Other than that, there are archeological sites about which there is various scholarly theories. It was not the purpose of our research to look into the extended history of architectural heritage in Kosovo. Our primary goal was to assess its current state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The oldest site of the Ottoman period is the Imperial Mosque in Pristina, from the fifteenth century, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's that one. There's also at least one mosque in Vucitrn which is roughly of the same era. There is an even earlier mosque which is in the vicinity of Mitrovica, near Trepce, which is now an archeological ruin. What one calls Ottoman or Albanian is a matter of judgement, as we discussed yesterday. A lot of the village mosques display the signs of the local architecture in the same forms; others display forms brought from elsewhere. This is as true of mosques as it is of churches. Some of the early churches display signs of Byzantine architecture. Others are of a distinctive local style, more of a style of architecture; similarly with mosques.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I assume you're familiar with a fact that is well known in history, that on the basis of Turkish records, in Kosovo and Metohija, at the beginning of the sixteenth century, only 2 per cent of the population were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems to me we're getting a very long way from the subject matter of this case. Now, you can ask him about his report, and that's what he's here to give evidence about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this refers to the report, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're not to ask about this. It's going too far back and it's not of assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, you mention damage to architectural monuments, and you mention 500 towers, or kulla, as symbols of Albanian culture and ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that most of those kullas were built by the Turkish occupiers during the Ottoman Empire and that during revolts by Serbs, Turkish feudal lords hid in them and sought shelter in them, so these are like the Norman castle in the territory of England?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my understanding. The kullas, or tower houses, are particular to this part of the Balkans. They are most dense in the western part of Kosovo, which is known in Albanian as Dukagjinii plain and as Metohija in Serbian. There were also some in Northern Albania, in Western Macedonia, and parts of Montenegro and the Dalmatian Coast. Most date from the eighteenth and nineteenth century, and for a variety of reasons, especially in Kosovo, they had become synonymous with the local Albanian culture. They are occupied by members of extended families, often going back for generations in the same kulla or group of kullas. They are not commonly found in towns, which is where any Turkish population was concentrated, except for Pec, which has some urban kullas. That's all the background I think I need to give on kullas. As you know, in our study, we say that a very large number of these kullas seem to have been targeted for destruction during the recent conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But it means that you do not agree with this allegation, this statement that kullas are kind of military fortifications.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in any modern sense. They had small windows and on the ground floor they generally had storage space and, in the villages, even animals housed. Yes, they did serve a defensive purpose in traditional clan disputes and such. Against modern weapons, they don't really offer much protection. No new kullas have been built since World War II, with one or two exceptions, perhaps. It's a traditional architectural form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. If you do not know this, I wish to tell you that an Albanian historian, Mark Krasniqi, in a book he published in 1958 entitled "Kullas in Metohija," described kullas as military forts. That was his finding, a finding of an Albanian historian in a book he published in 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know about what this historian said or not, Mr. Riedlmayer? If not, just say not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've heard of the historian. Mark Krasniqi is well-known in Kosovo. I think what he's underlining here is the purpose that I described earlier. These served as refuges during local feuds in traditional times. But their primary purpose is residential.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when Turkey left the territory of Kosmat, when the Turkish occupation of Kosmat ended?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ottoman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This isn't a history lesson. Yes. What's the relevance of this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I am talking about Ottoman monuments of culture, and Mr. Riedlmayer is identifying them as Albanian monuments of culture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we're going to be assisted by this distinction. The witness dealt with it yesterday. Now, have you got any more questions about the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in the conflicts, Albanian terrorists used those kullas as firing positions for operations in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information on what happened in those specific places during the conflict. All I can record is what happened to the buildings. In a number of cases, however, we do have the statements of the owners of the kulla, who claim that they fled with their families to nearby mountainsides and watched as Serbian troops burned down their kullas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as their statements are concerned, that is common knowledge, but I assume it does make a difference how those kullas were destroyed, because you said you only established the damage. So it's important to know whether it was due to natural disasters or, in conflicts, if they were used as firing positions. So that part of the story does not appear to interest you. Am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The damage we saw was inconsistent with natural disasters. In almost all cases, there was -- there were signs of fire. In some cases, there were signs of blast damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that -- can one infer from that that they were damaged in the fighting that was going on?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it happened at that time, definitely. Whether or not it was as a result of an exchange of fire, that I can draw no conclusions about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When you're talking about destroyed kullas, do you believe that all of them belong to Albanians or did some of them belong to Serbs? And they're also part of the architectural heritage of the Serbs then who lived in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of urban kullas in Pec had Serb owners. Those were the only kullas in Pec that we found undamaged. In Pec in particular, we found a number of kullas surrounded by modern buildings that were untouched while the kullas had been burned out. So in short, the answer is yes, there were some kullas that were owned by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that the kullas that belonged to the Serbs were not damaged, for instance, I happen to have some examples here of a kulla such as the Kusko [phoen] or KOS kulla, Garica, Decani, which the Albanian terrorists razed to the ground and which belonged to Serb families. And they were also protected cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't dispute that. I was talking with reference to Pec before. In the case of Decani, virtually all of the Old Town was either damaged or destroyed. According to our sources, this happened mostly in 1998. The vast majority of the population, and therefore I assume the vast majority of the residents of the kullas, were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, you say that the largest medieval Orthodox religious sites were carefully protected by KFOR. At the same time, you admit, as you yourself wrote, almost 80 churches and monasteries between June and September 1999 were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see a contradiction there? How do you explain the fact that you're claiming that they were well-protected while at the same time under the auspices of KFOR, only in the period from June to September, which is a three-month period, 80 churches were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see a contradiction. The major sites I'm talking about are the ones that are listed in all the guidebooks and which are very well known, such as the monuments in Prizren, in Pec, Gracanica, Decani. These had KFOR dispatched to them almost immediately to protect them. They also had some advice from UNESCO on this and were provided with a list of sites, I believe by UNESCO, in the early months of the post-war situation. At the same time, the destruction that happened tended to happen in rural areas, very often in areas from which the Serb population had already fled, and KFOR, especially in the early months, tended to concentrate its forces in areas where there was still a minority population that was in need of protection. The most important medieval monument that was destroyed was the church in Musutiste. It's quite remote from the main roads, and it was not well published in the scholarly and popular literature, and so it did not get sufficient protection, and it was blown up in the early weeks after the war. Other than that, most of the other churches and monasteries that were attacked tended to be in very remote places. We urged UNMIK to increase protection even for sites which had been damaged in the hope that reconstruction would be possible if no further attacks occurred. We were concerned to document especially those sites about which documentation was not otherwise available, and so we concentrated our efforts on that. Given the remoteness of the sites, we took considerable risks at times, going into areas that had not been clearly demined and where there was a chance that we would encounter some danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying, but my question was: How is it possible that if KFOR wanted to preserve Serb religious sites and monuments of culture, that so many, and on such a large scale, were destroyed? So let me explain my question further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, this witness can't answer for KFOR. That's a matter for KFOR. All he can describe is what happened or what he saw when he made his report. He can't answer for the actions of others, or lack of actions for others, as you allege.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, Mr. Riedlmayer claims that these monuments of culture were carefully protected by KFOR in his report which he has submitted, so I'm asking him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which passage are you referring to in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 021001, he says that religious -- Orthodox religious monuments were carefully protected by KFOR. And as we have seen, in spite of that careful protection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Nice, can you find this for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're probably having the same numbering problem which Your Honour has. The page number given by the accused doesn't match the ones in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, have you got a page number at the bottom, on the right, 1 to 20-odd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have page 10 here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I know what he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the top paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you can explain that passage to us, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. What I explain is that the majority of the damaged or destroyed buildings were village churches, many of them built during recent decades. About 15 of them date from medieval period. And then what I say is that the major medieval Orthodox shrines, however, had been under close guard by KFOR and have not been affected, and I've already named which ones I consider the major ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you believe to be the reason that Albanian terrorists blew up and razed to the ground churches that were damaged in the NATO airstrikes, without KFOR protecting them? Did it occur to you that the purpose may have been to destroy traces of vandalism committed by NATO during those airstrikes?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we covered this already yesterday. We were talking about the churches near Urosevac, at Nerodimlje. We have no information that these churches had been damaged in NATO airstrikes. We do have information that they were attacked after the war by Albanians. Beyond that, I cannot speculate as to motives. The most I can do is what the rest of that paragraph says, namely, that in some areas, there was a real correspondence of destruction of Islamic monuments and then a tit-for-tat destruction of Serbian monuments in the same locality, and I list several of them. I could list others, like Suva Reka. In the case of Urosevac, there was a cluster of these destructions that happened in areas where there were no corresponding Albanian religious sites that had been destroyed. I have no idea why this pattern occurred. There is also a similar pattern in the area around Klina, just east of Pec, where a number of churches, most of them modern but some like this, older, were targeted after the war. I assume that in each case it had to do with ensuring the departure of the affected population: the destruction of the mosques to make sure the Albanians wouldn't come back, and the destruction of the churches after the war to ensure that the Serbs wouldn't come back. This, unfortunately, has been a pattern in much of the Balkan conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that more than 30 per cent of Christian monuments in the first category, which means from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century, were destroyed in the area of Metohija after the arrival of KFOR?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the 30-per-cent figure. Are you saying that 70 per cent were destroyed before the arrival?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm talking of the percentage share of the total number of first-class monuments in the area of Metohija, so 30 per cent of those monuments were destroyed after the arrival of KFOR. I'm not talking about the 70 per cent at all.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. All we can do, as far as the figures go, is what I cite here, which is that approximately 15 of the churches that we have documentation for dated from the medieval period. Practically every church that dated from the medieval period was on the protected list. Since the protected list included more than 200 Orthodox monuments, that's not 30 per cent, but we don't have a category breakdown as to first, second, third.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, probably the figures don't tally, and there's quite a bit of difference, and I think that some objective, professional team would be able to establish them. But do you happen to know - and I'm linking this to what you said when you said that everything was well protected - that the Albanian terrorists, on the 13th of June, towards evening, once again stormed the Devic monastery and fired, open fire, asked for money from the nuns and the monastery treasures, took away the material goods that they had, took tractors and petrol and all their other equipment, such as typewriters, their fax machine, and so on and so forth, and of course all the monastery treasures which they held? They kept the nuns locked up in a room. They beat the only clergyman, the only priest there. His name was Pops Rafim [phoen]. And that went on for 24 hours, without anybody intervening, despite the presence of KFOR. Can you qualify that as good protection for churches and monasteries by KFOR?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only what I read in news reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the nuns even died as a result of that torture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He cannot help about this. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the Albanian terrorists, towards the middle of July, 1999, after the arrival of the German KFOR forces, demolished, pilfered, and mined the Monastery of the Trinity and the Holy Bogoradica [phoen] in Musutiste, once again a world-class, A1-category-listed site?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Musutiste is the site that I had just mentioned a few minutes ago. Yes, I'm aware of it. It was widely reported. There are many photographs. We also have video footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the Albanian terrorists, after the arrival of the German KFOR forces, mined and razed to the ground the St. George site in Suva Reka from the fourteenth century, once again a world-class site, category 1?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. No. It was Recani in the Suva Reka municipality actually. The place was called Recani by Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's in our database, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that on the territory of the Prizren municipality, also after the arrival of the German forces of KFOR, that they demolished, burnt, mined, and destroyed churches and monasteries of St. Mark and the Holy Virgin dated back to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Sveti Ilija, Sveti Nikola, Sveta Petka, Sveti Jovan in Ljubiste, that is the sixteenth century, Sveti Vasilije The Great in Srbica, and St. Nicholas in the town of Prizren, dating back to the fourteenth century. Do you know about that? Have you taken note of all these things? And can we deduce from those incidents, because we're talking about the town itself here, that had KFOR undertaken anything to protect -- did KFOR undertake anything to protect these buildings and guard them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- you have a long list of monuments. I assume most of them are not in the town of Prizren. The one that you mentioned, the St. Nicholas, I assume is the school chapel which we do have recorded, which had an explosive placed in it. However, other Serbian monuments in Prizren we found to be intact and under guard. So we have recorded all of the monuments you've listed in our database. And in Prizren, we personally visited each of these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the Sveti Avrilo monastery in the Vitina municipality, dating back to the fourteenth century, also a world class category 1 site, after the arrival of the American soldiers, was set fire to and demolished and a fire was placed inside it, burnt from inside?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the sites we visited at considerable risk to ourselves. It was in October of 1999. It was damaged already. The church itself had had a fire set in it but was structurally not affected. The monastery konak, the residence, had been largely burnt out. Subsequent to our visit, according to the IMG report, which has a photograph, the church was blown up in December of 1999. I consider this to be a criminal act and I'm very sorry that it was not prevented. On our way out from that location, which is listed in our database under the place number Buzovik which is the closest village, we actually asked the KFOR post if a guard could not be sent up to the monastery to protect it. As far as I know, no action was taken. So in short, yes, we know about this site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you probably know about the localities and villages where the churches, monasteries, mosques were destroyed, and other cultural monuments and buildings of cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we hope so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you began your presentation by showing a small church to show that it had not been destroyed and that all the talk about the destruction is a fabrication. But as we know, the assertions that have been made about the destruction of hundreds of churches is not something that has been thought up. Is that correct? They actually exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does the question mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question means that great crimes were committed in -- not only over people but over cultural buildings and cultural heritage as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, have you got a question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Albanian terrorists, after the arrival of the French KFOR forces in mid-August 1999, demolished, burnt, and mined the church of St. George in Rudnik, which is Srbica, dating back to the sixteenth century?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Rudnik is listed in our database. But I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that once again terrorists, after the arrival of the Italian forces of KFOR in July 1999 demolished, burnt, and mined the church of the Virgin Mary in Dolac, St. Nikola in Kijev [as interpreted}, dating back to the fourteenth century, and once again the St. Nicholas church in Cabici, sixteenth century, near Klina? These are all world-site, category 1 monuments and sites.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with these sites. In the case of Dolac, we actually provided photos of the destruction to the Serbian Orthodox eparchy, which they display on their website.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All this is well known and you have found it to be so in the manner in which I describe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the manner in which it's described in our report, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the terrorists, after the arrival of the British units of KFOR in June 1999, demolished and on the 17th of July 1999 mined and destroyed the church in Slovenia, which is the Lipljan municipality? It is the St. Nicholas church dating back to the sixteenth century.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the church of Slovenia was actually mined twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, once in June and the second time in July 1999. And do you know about the mining and destroying of the St. Nicholas church in Kijev [as interpreted], which is near Malisevo, also a world-class site, once again after the arrival of KFOR in the summer of 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the town's name is Kijevo, and yes, we have that recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you happen to notice, when you were visiting the area to establish the state of affairs, that the jeopardised zones, the threatened zones around the Decani monastery and the Ljeviska Obogorodica [phoen] and Pecka Patriarsija, Patriarchate, was because, with the acquiescence of UNMIK and KFOR, their blessing, they now disrupt the whole area by allowing houses to be built and shops, and to allow the land to be used as a waste area for refuge -- refuse?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are dealing with destruction, not general town planning issues. Now, can we move on, please, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the Albanian terrorists, after KFOR's arrival, destroyed tens of thousands of icons and iconostases and church artefacts and sacred items, an enormous number of books and relics, and a lot of that is being sold today illegally on the art market, black market, throughout the world? Do you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I not only have knowledge of that, I actually wrote about it in an article I published in the summer of 2000, about the appearance of artefacts clearly looted from churches in Kosovo on the art market. There was a news report of somebody in Tesovaniki [phoen] who was caught with artefacts that clearly came from churches in Kosovo. This is an unfortunate fact that has happened in all of the wars in the Balkans, that, quite aside from any political motives, the biggest driving force is that of simple human greed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So looting, you say. On the 24th and 25th of March, you spent some time in Kosovska Mitrovica and on that occasion you went to the municipal library there.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the by, people, the Serbs lived behind barbed wire in that part of the world, but that is not the subject of your study. But could you explain this: Why on the 24th of March suddenly you interrupted a meeting of the Serb and Albanian librarians in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not interrupt the meeting. I was present at the meeting. The meeting was interrupted because a crowd was gathering outside the library and the two Serbian librarians feared for their safety, and so they were taken back to the north side. The next day, I visited them on the north side and then carried out the assessment at the library on the south side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't precise enough. I didn't say that -- and mean that you personally interrupted the meeting. What I meant was that you, in the sense of those taking part in the meeting, that the meeting was interrupted because of the violence that was organised in front of the library. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether there is any institution or professional one of the -- of professionals of Serb ethnicity who stayed on working in Kosovo in that region, except Kosovska Mitrovica, dealing in the subject of the protection and safeguarding of cultural heritage? Is there anybody still there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cultural heritage I have no knowledge of any that stayed. I do know that in Gnjilane municipality there's some cooperation with librarians, Serbian librarians in the enclaves, and the director in Gnjilane, who is an Albanian. As far as the Institute for the Protection of Monuments, the Serbian staff left in June of 1999 and took most of the records of the Institute for the Protection of Monuments with them to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Do you know of a single Serb working there, except in Kosovska Mitrovica? And as I can see, there aren't any there. Now, do you know whether that in the centre of Pristina, immediately after the arrival of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that or not, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can briefly say yes, I do know that the Serbian Orthodox Church has been trying to organise the salvage of artefacts that were rescued from burned-out churches, and I had some correspondence with Father Petar Ulemek of the Pec Patriarchate on this subject, but that is the only thing I know about this. It's really outside of the subject of our study.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked about a professional working there, not any member of the clergy. The clergy carry on their own business. Now, do you know that in the centre of Pristina, immediately after the arrival of KFOR, the Albanian terrorists destroyed the monument to Petar Petrovic Njegos and Vuk Karadzic and on that spot they erected a monument to the well-known terrorist and killer Jasari?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The erection of monuments is not something that we looked into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that after the arrival of the German contingent of KFOR in Prizren, the monument to Tsar Dusan, a medieval ruler, was destroyed, who had his seat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He didn't look into the monuments. Do you know anything about this particular monument?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I know is what I read on the Serbian Orthodox Church's website, which has a little picture of it, but as I said, we did not, as a matter of principle, look at certain categories of things such as archeological sites, public statues, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in those localities, as cultural heritage was protected, does that include the old part of Prizren, Potkaljaj, which was inhabited by the Serbs, and after KFOR's arrival, this was destroyed by the Albanian terrorists in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We visited Prizren and went up to that neighbourhood which I believe is the one you're talking of. It's up the hill from the Catholic cathedral, and we observed some old houses that had been burned out and we were told that they were houses of Serbs. We did record that in our database.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had several questions regarding monuments, but I understand that that was not in your field of expertise, so let me ask you this: Do you know about an article by Robert Friske [phoen] published in the London Independent on 20th of November, 1999 which speaks of the destruction of Serb churches by the Albanian terrorists, along with the support of KFOR? Have you read or heard of that article? It was published in The Independent and it speaks about the destruction of Serbian churches along with KFOR support.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to follow the media. I vaguely recall reading the Friske article -- the Fisk [phoen] article. It mostly seemed to speak of items that we had covered in our survey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these findings of yours relate to the consequences of war, as far as I'm able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not natural catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you understand that your previous government, in that war against Yugoslavia, introduced the largest war machinery of 19 NATO-pact countries?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not for the witness. We have been over it yesterday. It's nothing to do with the witness. Now, Mr. Milosevic, even if you're right, supposing you're right for a moment, for the sake of the argument, and there was considerable destruction of Serb churches, Serbian Orthodox churches, and the witness accepts that there has been, what the indictment charges is the destruction of various mosques and other such cultural monuments. Now, then, how does it assist for you to put a large number of allegations about other destruction? What this Tribunal is concerned with is what's in the indictment. What the witness has given evidence about is general destruction, and you've asked questions about it, but what you have to concentrate on is what's in the indictment. Those are the charges you've got to answer. Now, have you got any more questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking here, Mr. May, about the consequences of war and not about which side did what, but the consequences of war, because the consequences and the results of war are the damages that were done both on Serbian, Islamic, Catholic churches, monuments, and so on and so forth. And there was a war, and the war was caused by the NATO alliance and not Yugoslavia, because Yugoslavia did not attack itself, but NATO attacked Yugoslavia. And you're trying here to use fractions and parts of war and set them aside from the whole and then to accuse those whom you consider to be responsible for those fractions and parts. But when I speak about the lack of evidence, about the destruction, of damage done to Serbian churches, I want to show the biased nature of this study, because we're talking about the consequences of war here, which was provoked by the NATO-pact aggression. But yes, I do have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about cooperation with Harvard, and I assume that you know what the press is writing, the Boston press, because Boston is the cultural headquarters of America. And let me quote just one paragraph from an article, which I suggest that all those present here read. It appeared in a Boston newspaper, and it says the following: [In English] "Surrounding the Milosevic trial is meant to distract us from the reality of our Balkans misadventure when we went to war not against --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This has nothing to do with the witness. Comments in a Boston newspaper have nothing to do with them. Now, have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you any questions about his report and his evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of his evidence, yes. Mr. May, it does have to do with his testimony. And even now, when the press of America says: [In English] "... not against terrorism but in its behalf," [Interpretation] that we went to war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with the evidence of this witness. Now, unless you have another question, relevant question, I'm going to stop this examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this does have something to do with the fact that Mr. Riedlmayer is testifying here. He is testifying here about something that is already common knowledge in America, that it was war in the name of terrorism and not against terrorism, which means that I'm asking Mr. Riedlmayer whether he understands that this false Tribunal here is a continuation and a consequence of that war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper question. Right. That's the end of that. No, I'm not going to allow this to go on. Do the amici have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. In my attempt to clarify a few points, I shall make very minor digressions and shall focus exclusively on what is contained in Mr. Riedlmayer's report. So I should like to begin from paragraph 4.0, page 11, which contains data on the c.v.'s of the main researchers. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question first, Mr. Riedlmayer, if I have read this correctly, and I think I have: In the second paragraph of the biographies of the principal investigators, it says that you are a master of social sciences and a master of the natural sciences, that you have these master degrees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have an MA in Near Eastern Studies and MS in Library and Information Science.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But neither you nor Mr. Herscher do not have a doctor's degree?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a doctoral candidate. Mr. Herscher's Ph.D. is expected next month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But regardless of that, you certainly have very high education. But it is not in the area relevant to architecture, art, painting, but rather, social sciences.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I've worked for 17 years as an art documentation specialist. I have taken advanced courses in this. I've written articles on art documentation, as you will see in my c.v., and although my training at Princeton and at Chicago was as a cultural historian, certainly material culture and architecture were part of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It also says in your c.v. that you mainly did your research in Islamic architecture and that you are a recognised expert on the cultural heritage of the Ottoman era, Balkans.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know very well - and that is why I'm asking you this - that prior to the Ottoman era, there was the Byzantine era and the time of Orthodox history, and then after the Ottoman period, there was another hundred years of history. So in addition to the Ottoman era, there was the Byzantine period, then the medieval Serbian state, and then after the Ottoman era comes another hundred years of history; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and although it's not stated in the short biography, I had a minor in Byzantine Studies when I took my undergraduate degree, and I've been studying the history of the Balkans, both pre- and post-Ottoman as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained to us yesterday that the idea occurred to you to study this problem, which is certainly worth attention of any human being. You decided yourself, you found sponsors, and you came to The Hague and offered your services. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would need to address you at this point in time and to make an objection, not a comment, regarding this. And the objection is that the prosecution, anywhere in the world, of course, if a crime is being investigated, looks for experts itself from various areas, designates them, and entrusts them with a particular task, and in this case - and I must make an objection to this procedure - somebody came here who had the funds secured, who had already done part of the job, and offered his own services. So I think that this is not in accord with certain basic principles that apply everywhere in the world, because the prosecution and the courts designate the experts themselves for this kind of work. I have no question regarding that. I just wish to make that remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What difference does it make?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The difference is that in this way, a complete impartiality would have been ensured, because otherwise it means that anyone who secures the funds can offer his services to an institution of this kind, and I think that in this case, the Prosecution should have selected among the numerous experts a particular one who would study this problem. That is my remark, and not a question. May I continue with my questions now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let me say this, since you've made what you call an objection: that we've heard the evidence. It will be for us to assess what weight to give this witness's evidence, but he's made his explanation as to how he came to draw up this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That goes without saying, Your Honours, and I know that the Court is here to provide the answers to all the questions. I thought it was my duty to make this observation because I feel it needed to be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question has to do with the following: On the cover page of your report, it says: The damage done to sites in Kosovo. That is the first page of your report: "The destruction of cultural heritage in Kosovo," on the front page. And on the second page, it says: "The destruction of cultural heritage in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999," so it's slightly different. I understand that specific damage -- to assess specific damage, you have absolute qualifications required, but who determined the frameworks of your expertise? Did somebody give you an assignment to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can see, both the front page and the inner page talks about the framework 1998-1999. We determined that ourselves, given that the first allegations surface in late May of 1998 and continue through the summer of 1999. So we decided upon the temporal parameters ourselves, having to do with the fate of cultural heritage in a situation of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you yourself came to the conclusion that your educational background gives you the capability to study all this and research it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I consider myself equipped, as does Mr. Herscher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to raise two issues? I will not enter into a discussion of matters outside the report but only things contained in the report. But precisely because the Prosecution, on page 1661 from the LiveNote, when the Prosecution asked a witness, the Prosecution asked a witness a question about a mosque destroyed in the seventh century -- no. A mosque from the seventh century apparently destroyed in a village. So please check the transcript, page 1661. The reference was to a seventh-century mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question to this witness is: Is he aware of any mosques existing in that area in the seventh century?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this must have been either a translation problem or something else, because "seventeenth" would make sense. "Seventh" makes no sense whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you. But as Mr. Slobodan Milosevic referred to this, allow me to ask you: When you were in the area, did you examine a church in Prizren, the church of the Holy Mother Ljevicka?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what fate befell it? Do you know what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were there, it was surrounded by razor wire and it had KFOR stationed around it. We observed some broken windowpanes, but otherwise the church was in good condition, as far as we could tell. We could not gain access to the interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you whether you know what happened to it. Do you know that it was the first mosque that the Albanians made in Kosovo out of a church, that originally it was a church turned into a mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, throughout its long history, it was a mosque far longer than it was a church. It was built as a church during the medieval Serbian kingdom. Upon the Ottoman conquest, as the principal church in Prizren, it was converted to a mosque. After the Balkan wars, when Serbia took Kosovo, it was reconverted into a church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Riedlmayer, when I received your report again yesterday, I was afraid of making a mistake, so I looked through it very carefully, and I focused in particular on the photographs. And on all the photographs, you have exclusively photographs of damage to monuments of the Ottoman period. There is not a single photograph in this report of what happened to other cultural monuments. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photographs that are appended here are photographs of items mentioned in the indictment. This is by no means representative of the entirety of our report. This is merely a sample that happens to correspond with the sites specifically mentioned in the amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after all, in the Prosecution, they did tell you to focus only on the monuments that were monuments from the Ottoman period that were destroyed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Our report, as submitted, ends before the pictures. The pictures were added as an aid to the Court just in the -- in the run-up to the trial here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you went there --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but you said that you went there in the autumn of 1999 to establish which cultural monuments - Islamic, Orthodox, Catholic - were destroyed. Why, then, did you not include here, for instance ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 19, Your Honours, for instance, paragraph A2.4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here that as a source, you used the book "Crucified Kosovo." Did you have this booklet?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, when we started, most of the contents of "Crucified Kosovo" was on a website set up by the Decani monastery. Subsequently, we exchanged photographs with Father Sava, and "Crucified Kosovo" appeared in an enlarged edition about a year later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you if you had all those photographs available from which it can be seen where which KFOR force was stationed. Why didn't you include some of those photographs in your report? Because these too are cultural monuments and you went there to study all cultural monuments.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in our database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the entire report of the witness, with the 500 pictures and the entirety of the survey, is on the CD-ROM that was disclosed to the amici a long time ago. Those are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, there is no mystery about this. The witness has told us that the photographs he has included yesterday were those which relate to the indictment. It sometimes is forgotten in this case that the case is being tried on an indictment. And those were the photographs which were selected. There's no mystery to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honours, rather, I understand what you're saying to me, and I quite agree with you, but the problem emerges from the actual finding and what the witness has said. He went there to survey all the damage and the destruction done to all heritage in Kosovo and Metohija. In this report, he refers to those things in writing without providing photographs. But I am satisfied with the answer. The important thing is that I drew attention to it. What I am interested in is the following:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the report says that about 80 Serbian churches were destroyed, and you say that you did have in mind the data contained in this book, here they refer to 107 churches. Why did you not accept this fact found in this document that you had access to? A hundred and seven churches. In your report you mention about 80.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two constraints, one of which was that our time frame ends with October of 1999, and the second one, that we did not include any documentation for which there were no photographs available. If you look at "Crucified Kosovo," you will see that a number of churches are mentioned by name but there is no photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but the figure is 107 churches, and data about them are given; location, under whose protection they are, when, what happened, and so on.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we made it a principle not to include items in our database which did not have some photographic evidence. We -- this was merely a conservative way of approaching documentation. We did not believe allegations necessarily without some corroboration, either a second independent source or photographs, preferably both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you toured 144 sites. How many of these sites were linked to the cultural heritage of the Catholic and Orthodox people?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an exact count, but I think we did something around 50 of Christian sites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to refer to some of the assessments that you made in your report. In paragraph 1.2 on page 2, you said sometimes that political criteria were important when something was decided to be a cultural heritage site, but here you use a different expression. You mentioned ideological considerations with respect to cultural monuments. Can ideological considerations be taken into account at all with respect to cultural monuments?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I consider in this sense political and ideological to be related if not synonymous. Secondly, what is and what is not considered an important cultural monument is in all cases a value judgement. The value judgements can have a variety of criteria. What I'm saying is that, from the statistical breakdown, it seemed quite evident that Serbian monuments were more heavily represented in the officially protected list than non-Serbian monuments in Kosovo. This had certain consequences with regard to the actual protection offered to them, which is not really relevant to our study. What is more relevant to our study is the fact that if we had concentrated exclusively on the officially listed monuments, we would have missed out on a large number of unlisted monuments that are historically or culturally important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that and there is some logic to that, but if they didn't have this footnote -- you said that your explanations regarding ideological considerations has to be understood in the context of the footnote number 3, and in that footnote number 3, it says: [as read] "By the time of the outbreak of the 1998-1999 conflict, some 210 Serbian Orthodox monuments (churches, monasteries, cemeteries) in Kosovo had been granted listed status, including 40 churches built between the 1930s and the 1960s [sic]. In contrast, in contrast, only 15 of the more than 600 mosques in Kosovo were listed as historic monuments, even though more than half of these mosques date from the Ottoman era." So you're asking how is it possible that so few mosques were protected? And there were 600 of them. But you have completely forgotten something else: The fact that in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, there are at least 1.300 Serb monasteries. There are authors that give the figure of 1.400, 1.600, but there were at least 1.300. There are ample books about this. Perosacro [phoen], an Italian author, for instance, but let's not go back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have a question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say all this because if the criterion with respect to ideological considerations was the number of mosques, why the number of churches was not given? Why this difference in approach? Why was it not established how many churches there were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. Let the witness answer. It's gone on for two minutes, this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the question was regarding the number of churches. The reason we could not come to a figure regarding the number of churches is because the statistics Mr. Tapuskovic cites generally refer to any Orthodox structure that may ever have existed in Kosovo, whether it's an archaeological remnant or something merely mentioned in a monastic charter. Our survey was strictly limited to actual standing buildings. And the number I cite of 210 Serbian Orthodox monuments are standing buildings, not archaeological sites that were on the officially protected list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm referring to. There are still 1.300 churches in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. This is a fact that you didn't have. At this moment, there are more than a thousand churches, not 210 that are protected, on the protected list based on UNICEF's [as interpreted] criteria, but churches that still exist. Obviously, you do not have that fact.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe the figure is correct. I think the number of actual intact buildings is considerably smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something else. In paragraph 2.2 of your report, where you said that it appears that the purpose of those attacks, and you're referring to sites of Ottoman -- the Ottoman period, that the aim was to destroy buildings and mosques and religious buildings related to the Albanian population of Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was the same not said of what happened to cultural monuments of the Orthodox church after the war, when the war was over? You said this only in relation to Albanian monuments. Why didn't you say the same with respect to what happened to Orthodox cultural monuments?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I say something of this sort in the paragraph 2-5 -- 2.5 where I speak of the post-war destruction of Orthodox monuments. I think it goes without saying that a Serbian Orthodox monument is associated with the Serbian presence in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. You made an assessment here. You said that this was done because they were Albanian buildings and that that was the purpose. But with respect to the destruction of monuments of the Orthodox faith, you did not say that the same purpose was behind it. So you didn't adopt an equal approach to the problem, an equal-sided approach.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is very clear. You expressed an opinion with respect to Albanian monuments, and you said it appears that the aim was to destroy those buildings. Why didn't you say the same when you established what had happened to Orthodox monuments and Catholic monuments and buildings too?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say as much, I thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. This is a matter for us to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That is precisely why I'm doing this, to draw your attention to it. The same applies to something on page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got very much more for this witness, Mr. Tapuskovic? It's 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another ten or 15 minutes. I will finish very quickly after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: After the adjournment. We will adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will really try to be as brief as possible and just ask a few more questions. I have made a selection, and I won't go back to some of the issues, but just to wind up what I was saying and with respect to something that is contained in Mr. Riedlmayer's report. It is paragraph 2.4 this time. In that portion of the report, he makes a statement, an assessment: The army of Yugoslavia, at the beginning of the NATO strikes, used as military facilities -- which represents violations of the laws of war analogous to misuse of the Red Cross symbol. That paragraph. So that is an assessment that Mr. Riedlmayer makes, that paragraph. Now, was he able to say that just by having examined the buildings or is it something that he learnt through his contacts in the field and then introduced that into his report?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you answer that question, please, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. In both cases, the case of the Catholic Church of St. Anthony in Pristina and the Catholic church in -- I'm sorry. The Catholic Church of St. Anthony in Pristina and the St. Anthony Catholic Church in Djakovica, the information came from the local parish priest, and it was duly noted as such in the entries for those monuments. In the case of the church in Djakovica, the only traces of the occupation was the fact that the friary was being repainted, and the priest told us that that was as a result of vandalism. Clearly, we did not see any visible evidence of what had happened during the war. We merely transmitted the statements of these two priests, both of whom lived through the war in those locations, and their statements are identified as such, as our source of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you considered that an assessment of that kind should be included into that report, and I can agree with that. When you went to see the representative of the Serbian Orthodox Church, did you ask them perhaps about whether some of the buildings dating back to the Ottoman Empire had not perhaps been used at one time or another for these same purposes that you mention here? Did you ask somebody to explain that to you perhaps, or did anybody say anything in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what your question is. You said: Did we ask representatives of the Serbian Orthodox Church about Ottoman, I assume you mean Islamic, monuments. And the answer is no. We asked them about Serbian monuments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Here you make an evaluation, an assessment, and say that the Yugoslav army troops used it as a military facility. Now, did you talk to anybody else when it came to damages of Orthodox churches and monuments -- no, mosques first. I misspoke. Mosques. That mosques were used, that mosques had been used for war purposes, military purposes, especially the kullas?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The kullas were residential architecture, not mosques. And no, we had no information about any military uses of mosques.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking whether, in the field, just like you talked to the Catholic priest here, did you talk while you were over there with a Serb representative who could give you some facts and figures and information along the lines of my question? So if you make this kind of assessment in this paragraph, why did you not take the trouble to find out about the other aspect and then introduce an assessment, as you did this one here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we were merely transmitting two eyewitness reports by the parish priests regarding the churches which were their own church. We did not ask for, nor did we place much reliance upon, general statements of any sort. Our primary goal was to make observations of our own, and then if eyewitnesses with specific information related to those sites came forward, we would take their statements in a general form. With regard to the Serbian Orthodox Church, as I indicated in my testimony, we engaged in extended correspondence with Father Savo Janjic and with Father Petar Ulemek of the eparchy of Raske in Prizren. We tried to meet them in October 1999, but they were out of the country for a conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you this: If you talked about the fact that some facilities had been used as military facilities, that some buildings had been used as military facilities, why, when you talked to the Serbian representatives, did you not inquire as to whether some buildings were used for military facilities, such as the kullas, if you knew about academician Mark Krasniqi, and according to him, that the kullas were generally used, in addition to being places of residence, for war purposes, and it says there that they were also used in cases of defence, in a blood feud or in fighting a foe, an enemy. So were you interested in learning whether those kullas were being used for military purposes, as military facilities?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Collecting that kind of information, asking those kinds of questions, was not really our primary goal. We were there to record the buildings. If eyewitnesses approached us, the only question we would likely ask them is: Did you see what happened to this building, and can you briefly tell us what you know about it? That was the extent of our investigation as far as eyewitness statements goes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer, for that. I'm just asking you why you included an assessment which did not have to do with what you were doing there, what your job was there. This is an assessment that steps outside the framework of your expertise and interest. That's all I'm asking you. Thank you for your explanation, because you did not follow the same pattern in some of the other parts of your report. Mr. Slobodan Milosevic -- and I have to go back to that because he was interested in it - spoke about and asked you a number of questions here, but I'm not going to go back to them, that has not been challenged, that none of the important Orthodox monuments were directly hit by a NATO bomb. However, another question is far more interesting, and can you give us -- say something on the subject? The foundations, the foundations of these important historical monuments, especially fresco paintings, and the airstrikes. Now, did you focus on whether there were any damages done to the frescoes? You, of course, know what frescos are and how fragile they are and how they survive miraculously through the centuries, but how they could be destroyed from an -- by an airstrike or bomb exploding or an explosion of any kind? Did you focus your interest on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as I mentioned in my testimony, given that all we could do is make a visual inspection, we relied upon statements from two paintings conservation experts. One is Ms. Tody Cezar, who did the assessment as an independent consultant to UNMIK of a number of Orthodox and Islamic sites that had fresco paintings. The other one were -- was an Italian team that visited sites in Pec and Decani. And their conclusions was -- were that they saw no evidence of war damage. What they did see was evidence of damage from rising groundwater. You could feel the walls, and they were wet. This is something that can be easily remedied through intervention, but if left alone, it will damage the frescoes. Whether or not shaking can injure building, without a doubt it can, but that kind of analysis requires tools and expertise that we did not have at our command. That's why we rely on the statements of experts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to weary Their Honours or anybody else in the courtroom, but just one thing: When you went to Gracanica, Gracanica is right by Pristina, and it's a very important monument to one and all in the world and of course for the Serbs especially, but it is the cultural heritage of mankind. Now, were you interested, when you went to visit it, in hearing what happened to Gracanica? Did they show you, from the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, the people from there, did they show you this photograph, for example, Mr. Riedlmayer, this one here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the photograph placed on the ELMO, please, with the usher's assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the monastery of Gracanica, Sveti Jovan Pretica. There's a crack, but those cracks go deep down into the foundations of the church itself.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that this is the book published in the spring of 1999 by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Republic of Serbia. We saw this book, and we looked at the walls. There were a number of cracks in the walls. Many had been repaired back in the '60s and '70s using concrete plaster which is now considered inappropriate material for this kind of purpose. Whether or not the crack is bigger or smaller than it has been before, we had neither the documentation nor the expertise to judge. Certainly I was there in October 1999 rather briefly. My colleague Mr. Herscher made several repeat trips to Gracanica. In addition, Ms. Cezar went and did an assessment, and it did not seem that the building was in any danger. Furthermore, the monks at no stage mentioned any war damage. Again, the problem at Gracanica was rising damp from groundwater.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm happy to hear that you have seen the book. I think it's translated into English. And it says that it has been ascertained that those cracks seriously damaged the very foundations of the church. Now, did you read about that? Have you read that or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as I say, that is one assessment. The experts we consulted said something else. And we would have expected the local monks to tell us about the damage, war damage, if there had been any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They couldn't have known at that point in time, but thank you for your answer. I'm satisfied with your answer. You said yesterday in testifying that -- that when -- you testified in front of the OSCE about the destruction of the cultural heritage. Why and when did you testify before the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in April of 1995. It wasn't the OSCE but the Congressional Committee on Security and Cooperation in Europe. It's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... about Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That has nothing to do with what I've just asked you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I just have two matters. Re-examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, during cross-examination you have been asked to deal with several examples of allegations of destruction or damage of specific religious sites, and at that time you did not have your report with you. And with the permission of the Court, I would ask you to complement, if necessary, and very briefly, by using the photographs or any of your material the answers that you gave yesterday. I will refer to some of the --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I turn this on?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I have some help somehow? Can Mr. Riedlmayer have some help? Maybe -- I have here an investigator that is familiar with the computer and the database.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this is our database, and the format is something that should be familiar from the sample sites that we submitted. So which sites were you interested in?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will refer to the ones that were put in front of you by the accused.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, there was an allegation that the Pec Patriarchate was hit by the NATO planes, and you answered by saying that you visited that site and found no sign of damage other than rising damp and long-term deferred maintenance.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- do you feel the need of adding or --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can show you the site record that we have for it. It's coming through. Okay. So here we have no external sign of damage seen in October 1999. At that time, KFOR did not permit access to interior. Mr. Herscher subsequently visited also and conservator Tody Cezar carried out an assessment of the interior murals, found damage from rising damp due to groundwater seepage and from pre-war restorations carried out using inappropriate materials but did not see sign of war damage. She also mentioned to me again that she was guided around by a Serbian guide who made no reference to war damage. The photo comes from a KFOR website, just showing an Italian soldier in front of the monastery. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. Another one would be the Gracanica monastery --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Generally, by the way, it was a problem that KFOR, for various reasons, did not permit photography of these buildings, and so we had to rely on outside sources. In the case of Gracanica, we have post-war photographs from the Serbian Orthodox eparchy. So we saw no sign of damage during our visit in 10/99. Mr. Herscher also subsequently visited Gracanica, and Tody Cezar made a very similar observation to what she did in Pec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, it was alleged by the accused that the area of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Gracanica monastery was bombed by NATO several times and that the rockets might have damaged the site. Do you -- did you find any evidence of that when you --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- visited?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the outskirts of Gracanica, there was a major Yugoslav army base which was hit during the war. I don't exclude the possibility that the building might have been shaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you visit, did you see signs of any damage?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we saw no signs of damage. Obviously, we were not able to do things like erect scaffolding and make technical examinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Another site that was put for you was the Gazimestan complex, which is in the north of Pristina, and it was also alleged that the NATO planes directly target the memorial complex.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait. I'm sorry. This is -- the turbe of Gazimestan, after whom the location is named, which is on a hilltop across from the battlefield monument. Let me try this again. Okay. Here's the Spomenik Kosovskim Junacima, the Kosovo Battlefield monument. You can see it was built in 1953, renovated in 1989. Here's a photo of the only damage we saw. I'm sorry it's a little dark on the screen. These are these cut-off concrete tubes that were erected around the monument for the 600th anniversary. They hold spotlights, and they used to have these wrought iron ornaments on them which someone had ripped off. We were also told that inside the monument -- and here is the picture of the monument that actually I took. The monument, as you can see, is intact, but in the back of the monument is a door leading to an interior staircase which we were told had been damaged by explosives, but we were not allowed inside. But again, the door was intact, the stair apparently was damaged, but the exterior of the monument showed no damage other than the ripped-off cast iron ornaments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you visited the structure and the monument, everything was intact?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. This was in October of 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: October of 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Another site, Mr. Riedlmayer, would be the Catholic Church of St. Anthony in Djakovica, also alleged to be hit by the NATO airplanes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Here's the church. It was built in 1884, during the late Ottoman times. And it gives our assessment that the damage was limited to broken windows from air blasts. There's a Yugoslav army base only a couple of hundred metres behind the church, in the direction of the steeple there, and -- I'm sorry. In the direction of the apse, opposite the steeple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we see the computer monitor which the witness is watching? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
