utterances.text: I'm sorry. We were told that the windows were broken by the priest, and it was easy enough to confirm because there were new windows in with unpainted frames. If you look below, we have the statement of the parish priest, Father Ambroz Ukaj, which we took from him during our visit, where he says: On 24 March, half an hour before the first NATO airstrike, Yugoslav army troops ejected the priests and the nuns from the parish house and the church and took it over and stayed there for two and a half months. And the priest stayed in Djakovica throughout the war. He returned to the friary at the end of the war and found the parish house looted, with computers and other equipment gone, and some vandalism, and they were busy trying to repair it when we were there in October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next one would be the old marketplace of Pec, that was also alleged by the accused to be hit by the NATO several times and was also alleged to be completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Here we have the old marketplace in Pec. This is one of the places where we were able to get both before and after shots. You can see that, along entire streets of the market, the stores had been destroyed by burning, and we saw bulldozer tracks. Apparently the shops had been bulldozed. But behind the burned and bulldozed buildings, there was an intact row of buildings, and this extended for several blocks. Okay. Below, you see further destruction of the same sort. Here, on one side of the street, the buildings are intact; on the other side, they are burned and bulldozed. And behind it, although you can't see it on this photo - we have other photos - the buildings are intact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, according to your assessment, the cause of the damage would be what?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any other site that you have a recollection that you would need your database to --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can mention one more that Mr. Milosevic asked me about, which was the church at Dolac. Dolac is on a hilltop overlooking the Klina Valley, just off the main highway, but you have to go up a long dirt path to get there, and we were rather worried about mines. You can see the post-destruction photo on top is by Mr. Herscher. To orient yourself, you can see in the bottom picture, just to the left of the church, which is the white building, is a tree, which you can see also in the top picture. The rubble is that of the church, which, according to the Serbian Orthodox authorities, was blown up in the month after the end of the war. We went and found fragments of painted stonework and the slate roof. It was destroyed. This is one of the photos that we supplied to the Serbian Orthodox eparchy for their website. Below here is another pre-war picture from an official publication from the 1960s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Romano, since these sites have been put in issue, it would be helpful to have a printout of these reports, if the witness could assist the Prosecution when he's finished giving evidence. We'll have an additional report similar to the one that you have for the sites in his report, covering, I suggest, those sites mentioned specifically in re-examination, and it can be Exhibit 88A, and if you could produce it as soon as you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I also have here with me the CD-ROM that I mentioned -- that Mr. Nice mentioned yesterday, that contains the entire report and all the sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, are you asking to exhibit those?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes. It would be helpful for Your Honours to just -- it's easy to search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have the CD-ROMs. They can have the next exhibit number. But I suggest that the report which I've requested be 88A in any event, and this one can be the next one, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The CD-ROM will be numbered Exhibit 93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No problem. In addition to the CD-ROM, we'll provide another small report with the sites mentioned during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you need any specific programme to see the CD-ROM on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's a FileMaker database. I believe the Tribunal has a copy of the software, and the instructions for use are in the report here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes. We can provide anything that will be helpful to install the CD. I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, you mentioned that you did not include sites in the report that were no documentation, for which there were no photos available.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was referring to Serb sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was referring to all sites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To all sites. So Serb and non-Serb sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No more further questions, Your Honour. I just have just one matter that I think is outstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd like to also clarify that in the database, for technical reasons, there are sites for which we saw photo documentation but we could not include it. This mainly concerns the IMG database, which is password protected and so you can't move images out of it into another database.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, just one outstanding issue was about the exhibits that -- the photos and the map that Mr. Milosevic showed the witness and the witness dealt with yesterday, that I don't know if you want to -- if Your Honours want to raise that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure where they are. I think they may have gone back to the accused, in which case they can stay with him. I'll just ask the registry if they have them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, they're with the accused. It will be easier if they stay with them. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer, for coming to give your evidence. That concludes it. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient if we adjourn for ten minutes before dealing with the outstanding procedural matters. We'll begin with the Prosecution, the length of trial issue, and then go on with the other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ten minutes, until a quarter past. --- Break taken at 12.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it may be convenient, as I say, to take the issues, first of all, the Prosecution case trial estimate first, then to deal with the facilities for the Defence, including the Registry proposals, and finally, deal with the evidential issue about the binder. So we'll hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position I think at the moment is that as our paper, headed "Position in Relation to Management of the Trial," before the Chamber, seeks no immediate relief and simply identifies what we believe to be the present position and perhaps the present problems that we're all facing. The Chamber indicated at the beginning of the week that it would like some help from us in relation to estimates, and I think I responded at the time that a considerable amount of work was being done to try to bring realistic assessment to where we stand. In the event, because of the requirements of using tomorrow for a witness and advancing to today the hearing on procedural matters, the calculations of witness numbers have been done on all three parts of the indictment, but in a somewhat rough-and-ready way, and I'll come to that in a minute. But to summarise the position set out in recent filing, the Prosecution's view is that in light of the present and to some degree changed circumstances of the accused taking a full part in the trial, cross-examining fully and extensively, and in light of the decision that so far has been made about the use of 92 bis material, two things follow: One, that any earlier plan to call the most limited amount of material, which may have been possible if the accused had not been taking the part he has been, is a plan that now is redundant. And second, immediately following on the approach to 92 bis of the Chamber, other considerations may apply which will enable time to be saved. Before I move on to where we are and how we respectfully suggest matters can be dealt with, can I suggest for ease of understanding that the paradigm problem that we face in cases of this kind is that if, for example, you have a location, a village or municipality, where events happened for the proof of which there would typically be, say, ten witnesses who could give a complete view, can it ever be satisfactory simply to call one witness and have him fully examined and fully cross-examined and know nothing about or take nothing from the other nine simply because the overall time problems of the case make it difficult to hear anything of the other nine witnesses? And so it is that we've referred in our filing to the Chamber to the possibility of certain procedural steps which would enable the Chamber to become fully seized of all material that it would need or wish to be seized of, while saving an enormous amount of time compared with the time that would be consumed if every single relevant witness were taken fully. So that's, in summary, what the Chamber knows to be our position expressed in our paper. We go on to suggest that there are two ways in which the problem may be mitigated. First, by the use of summarising witnesses of a kind that have been used in other cases, dealt with at an early stage in relation to Kevin Curtis when the Chamber rejected his evidence, something to which we will wish to return fairly soon with the killing-site evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other cases you had in mind, Kvocka or Krstic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Where there was a summarising witness who reviewed the evidence overall and then a sample of the evidence was called. And so that's one technique which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So who do they call; an investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And he summarised the Prosecution evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, he did. And their reports -- I mean -- should I be turning it off each time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've been turning it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to make any complaint about that. We set out in the filing why this is desirable, but perhaps for the slightly wider audience that may be attending, I'll give the reasons again here with some concrete examples. First of all, if the time constraints of the trial are such that it's simply not going to be possible to take in full the evidence for each particular site that one would want to have taken, then if you just take the one witness or two, the Chamber proceeds in ignorance of what else, as it were, is available. If it hears a summary of what that other material amounts to, as I have suggested in the filing, that summary of material has three distinct potential values to the Chamber. First, the material may have some weight in itself to know that there are so many statements from so many witnesses given in a manner consistent with the live evidence may have some weight, and there's no reason to suggest otherwise. Second and perhaps, in a sense, of more value, it can provide a way of checking provisional or, indeed, final judgements of the Chamber if the Chamber could be satisfied from what it hears that there is no evidence significantly contrary to the evidence that it's already heard. The Chamber is thus, as it were, seized of all the material. Although it hears only part of it in detail, it's seized of all the material to that extent. And third, if it does decide that there is reason to be concerned about the effect of the Prosecution's evidence, it could either suggest that the Prosecution call more evidence on particular topics or, indeed, call more evidence itself. Can I suggest one example of how this evidence -- this approach to evidence might have been useful in the trial thus far and indeed useful to the accused in this particular example? In the early stages, there were one or two or it may have been several witnesses whose evidence to Your Honours was, to use an understatement, somewhat shy on the topics of the involvement of the KLA, and indeed it was revealed that they had said more in their witness statements about the KLA maybe than they said to Your Honours. Well, it happens that that was elicited in relation to the individual witnesses in court. But one can imagine how it would be helpful to the Chamber to know that, for example, what those witnesses had been saying about the KLA in their statements was matched perhaps by what other witnesses were saying about the KLA in their written statements. And it would be infinitely preferable on a topic like that that the Chamber should have that body of material before it rather than not to have it. So the summarising witness, in our respectful submission, is a witness that can leave the Chamber in possession of, seized of the material in a way that will be of value to it. It can attach some value to it, as I'm sure it did, I believe it did, in the judgement in Krstic. But its real value may be as a check or/and as a provider of information as to what other steps, if any, ought to be taken. There's another particular way in which summarising evidence may be of use in this particular trial. I've spoken thus far of the paradigm problem where you've got a location for whom you would normally want to call ten witnesses but the time constraints are going to make it desirable only to call one or two. The same problem exists where, for example, you're looking at the 47 municipalities currently charged in respect of Bosnia. Now, it may very well be in due course that by one route or another the Chamber is only going to be troubled with detailed evidence in relation to a smaller number of Bosnian municipalities. I'll come to this as a particular resolution quite shortly. If, for example, the Prosecution sought to prove its case in respect -- in detail in respect of only 25 of those municipalities, leaving on one side 22, there would always be the possible allegation that we had, in the vernacular of the age, been cherry picking. We'd simply been calling the best evidence which may have been wholly inconsistent with material elsewhere. Now, in those circumstances, summarising evidence given in relation to the other municipalities, summaries that of course could be checked by reference to the raw material by the amici or by those representing the accused would serve the same three purposes and have the same three values that I've already identified. First, it could be of some value in itself, bearing in mind the need to prove widespread and systematic conduct, but second, it could deal with any allegation that there had been a selection of material that was unfair or unrepresentative, and so it would serve that very considerable purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the answer to that potential criticism is that the Prosecution are under an obligation under Rule 68 to disclose any exculpatory material. So if it was said that a Prosecution was simply selecting the best evidence, why, the answer to that would be, Well, that's the Prosecution job, to select the best evidence. In any event, the interests of the Defence are protected by the requirement to disclose any exculpatory evidence. So speaking for myself, I don't see that that is a problem, the problem of selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Rule 68 obligation, which I was going to turn to at a later stage, is indeed an important bringer of some security to the Chamber and to ourselves in our separate functions, but on matters as wide in scope as the crime base, it's perhaps rather difficult to know exactly what is Rule 68 exculpatory. Particular events, yes, but the overall interpretation of a course of conduct, not so easy. And so although we for the Prosecution do two things, first, we attempt from the - I think in Kosovo 1.300 - witness statements that we have, to select what is a fair and proper representation of what happens in any particular area. And then secondly, we hand over - and we've had a recent exercise to ensure that this is done - we hand over under Rule 68 statements that are exculpatory. With the quantity of material and the wide nature of the issues involved, there's inevitably a sort of area of judgement, and we cannot be sure, as I have said, frankly, but as you select down to one witness per site or two witnesses per site, that we can really be getting something that is truly reflective of an overall history and situation. We do our best. We hope we get it right. But it is a very difficult exercise. Just let me make this point: The 68 exercise in relation to the 1.300 witness statements has led to the identification of the statements to be served. I think there is 105 that are now going to be served additionally. They haven't yet gone out. They will be going out I don't know how soon, shortly, but there are considerable problems about production of material in the Office of the Prosecutor. The advantage -- well, let me go on a little bit about summarising witnesses or witnesses who are able to review summaries of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a problem about the Albanian translation which will require some repair work, but I think we'll go on -- we can go on without the Albanian translation and get it done during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple more words about the summarising witnesses. There are summaries of -- various people are working on databanks of material in relation to all of these cases. We have seen them already. We've had, say, local witnesses who have their own collections of reports, the humanitarian witnesses, humanitarian group witnesses. We've had Dr. Ball and his evidence. And we know already of the existence of the OSCE report on which the accused has indeed been cross-examining, which in due course I may seek to lay before you before a witness. It's a report that, incidentally, deals with both sides of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, it sounds as though it would be helpful to have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have them already here and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In due course --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and in proper form, because, interrupting you for a moment, going back to your point of the summarising witnesses, it seems to me that reports of that sort may in fact cover, although not precisely the same, as I understand, but may cover a broader ground of material than the witnesses, and such reports have been, without controversy, I think, admitted in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we would certainly seek to lay those before you, and again, they serve, subject to the Court being satisfied as to the methodology of their preparation, they serve the same valuable purpose. So that, for example - and again, looking at it from the accused's point of view, because he so far has been relying on them - if, in relation to any particular location, we were to call evidence to a particular effect and the Chamber were to find from the OSCE report contrary conclusions, then that's the sort of material it might want to say: "Well, this requires further evidence, either you, the Prosecution, to deal with it, or alternatively, we, the Chamber, to deal with it." So it's that sort of material that's very valuable, in our respectful submission, or can be. And again, as I've said in the filing, if this approach is good, then it has to be good, of course, not just for documents that we might seek to produce, but again, subject to proof of methodology, documents that might come from the accused and have a different general approach. The overall advantage, and one that we respectfully suggest is extremely important, is that at the end of the exercise, it will not be possible for people to complain, either under any appeals mechanism or indeed elsewhere, that the Chamber hasn't been seized of all the relevant material and given it consideration, not necessarily all as live evidence, but at least given it consideration. And so with that in mind, and bearing in mind that what the investigators do is much the same as what is done by, for example, the OSCE, but on a more localised basis, we will be urging you in due course to take summaries of the witness statements prepared for the OTP for all those purposes and as part of the exercise of ensuring that the trial can be dealt with in a compact but nevertheless a proper way, that will give judgements of the Court sure foundations. Now, I know Your Honour was going to deal with the binder issue later, but may I respectfully invite you to deal with that now, because it touches the same issue and is another way of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- looking at the way we can move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that the Chamber had Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what I'm not sure is whether you have Bela Crkva in exactly the form that it's been served on the accused and on the amici. Because it may be that out of deference to the Chamber's concern at reading material it might not want to read, we may have excised one or two things. But I can tell you what's in a typical binder as we would propose to lay them before you. And if you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have it here, Mr. Nice, but we are familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have looked at it and I have notes on it, so I think I'll be able to follow what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. Your Honour, if the document -- well, again, for the wider audience that may be listening, and to follow what we're going to be suggesting now or at a later stage in the trial may save a lot of time: The location binder, municipality binder, village binder, whatever you like, driven really by civil-system dossiers but of course distinct from them, dealt with by the same Chamber, Your Honour's Chamber, differently composed, in the Tulica decision in the case of Kordic, is designed to allow procedures to operate in the following way: Sometime before the evidence would be called for the particular location - a few weeks, a month, or whatever it might be - all parties would be provided with -- or having been provided with the binder, would review in advance the evidence that would be called in relation to it. At that review, the Prosecution could explain what its position was, what witnesses it intended to call live or what witnesses it intended to adduce 92 bis, and so on. The accused would be in a position, as would the amici, to join in this exercise, and we suspect that it would be possible for the Chamber, even with an unrepresented accused, to narrow down with him the issues that were really live issues in respect of that site. I note parenthetically that the accused's response in relation to the Kosovo crime-base material may be different from the response that he will make in relation to the Croatia and Bosnia crime-base material, but we can't know that for some time to come. With that general introduction in mind, what the binder has on the first sheet is a simple, very short one-page summary of what the case is. Now, this is really almost like, as it were, an opening statement, where we could have read all of these out and got into trouble for going on too long in the opening, and it wouldn't have served much of a purpose. But it's basically a summary of the Prosecution's case in relation to that location, the Bela Crkva killing site, as it is described, and it can do no prejudice to the defendant to have the Prosecution's case identified at that stage, and must help. There then follows, in the case of Bela Crkva, 65 ter summaries of all, bar one, of the witnesses who we would intend to call - I'll deal with the one additional witness in a second - followed by, in each case, the original witness statement of that proposed witness. Well, of course the summaries are already available to the Chamber, but now they're collected together in a way that we hope will be helpful. Considering the statements, in our respectful submission, which is something that Your Honour and Your Honour's colleagues could do or could decide not to do until invited to do in a hearing or whatever, is not something that would embarrass the Chamber, being a Chamber of professional Judges, and indeed, as I understand it, other Chambers of the Tribunal are at the moment indeed taking possession of in order to read witness statements. But the statements are there, and the composition of the binder then follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The statements wouldn't be admitted as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just merely part of the background?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's part of the background. And so that if and when it's argued that Witness X adds to what Witness Y says in a material way and thus we need to call both of them, if that proposition is challenged, the matter can be immediately considered. If it's said that Witness X says something that's contradictory to what Witness Y says, and therefore the accused says he should be called, again, the Court is in a position to form a judgement on it straight away and decisions could be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are those statements coming in through the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Well, Your Honour, as I've -- as we just explored, they wouldn't be coming as evidence -- they wouldn't themselves be coming as evidence, but the next -- Your Honour is quite right in this: We then go beyond the table of contents, and the first witness statement is the statement of the summarising investigator, who would in all cases be the investigator who is closest to that particular location, who is -- typically, of course, more than one investigator will have taken statements and so on, but he would be the investigator who has been charged with looking at that site and dealing with it in detail. And in this particular case, although it's a very major crime and a very serious event on any reckoning, his summary is just over three sides. So again, it's a short summary. Basically it's, again, a summary of what is said and what's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is one thing, a summary of what's there and what is available. That is one thing. But evidence is another, and that surely is an important distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we were to admit the summary purely as that, and nothing more, for instance, as with the summaries of the witnesses we get - their summaries are not evidence - if we admitted that, that might be one thing, likewise the witness statements. The crucial thing is, of course, what we admit as evidence. Or may be the crucial thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed. Well, Your Honour, of course, if the witness, the summarising witness is called, and, for example, gives his evidence: "Well, I've gone through all the witness statements and they are broadly to this effect," and then he's cross-examined and he says, "Yes, it's quite true that these witnesses all, actually, in their statements acknowledge the presence of the KLA on the hill above so-and-so, even though only two of them were expected to be called," whatever it is. As I've suggested earlier, in each case, both in chief and in cross-examination, the evidence will have some value. I'm not shying away from that. And I think you'll find in Krstic, if we look at the way the evidence was dealt with there, and I haven't reviewed it recently, but I think you'll find that the summarising witness was referred to, and probably quite extensively. So I'm not going to dodge that column. But we would accept that the evidential value, if any, ultimately to be attached to the evidence of the investigator would be moderate at the most. But I'm not suggesting it doesn't have any value. Then the rest of the two rather large binders for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will then be asking us to take a slightly different view of the investigator's report from the one that we took in Tulica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. And as I've said in the motion, things have moved on from there, and also this case has its own particular difficulties and problems that we've simply got to face. Also, the practice of the Tribunal has developed, and we have these other cases to compare. But yes. And of course Your Honour, I'm sure, won't mind my saying this: The view was taken at the time, not necessarily in this Court, that these dossiers, if they had proved to be acceptable, could be one of the - at that stage - could have been one of the most efficient ways of saving time. There it is. I move on. The rest of the binder is self-explanatory. We've got some Rule 70 surrogate sheets, because that evidence hasn't yet met all its requirements; there are the individual exhibits; there's the exhumation reports, which I think under the Tulica decision the Chamber was prepared to accept in any event; and then there are a large number of photographs. So that to take this particular site, a major site in Kosovo, to understand what the Prosecution's case was, what the evidence available is, would take experienced Judges a really limited period of time to understand. It's been put together in a way to make ready access to the material. And with that understanding of the case and of what material is available, it's our invitation to the Chamber that we could then meet a few weeks before the Bela Crkva evidence would be given and say, in relation to it: "Well, we are proposing to call these two witnesses, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which would be our proposal, plus another witness who happens to have come up for consideration after this binder was prepared." But we would then say, "There's a third witness who we think probably doesn't need to be called because we can probably do without him, and the other two witnesses we would propose not to call." And subject to any representations that might be made by other parties, and although the Chamber, of course, wouldn't be expressly approving what we were doing or taking the decisions for us - I'll make that clear - we could then proceed either to call those witnesses or to call less of them or to call more of them, following on the decisions made by the Chamber. And in this way, the Chamber will, of course, have command of the unfolding of the evidence and of the timetable, and by drawing from the accused identification of what issues there are and what matters are not in issue, we will be able to save, I would hope, a very great deal of time. Now, incidentally, there's one thing I ought to say, and I keep meaning to say it and then keep forgetting it, so I'll say it now before I move to the next topic. The Chamber, having made the decision about how 92 bis should apply certainly thus far in this trial - that is, by statements being presented and the witnesses being subject to a few questions in examination-in-chief, and then to cross-examination, re-examination - has identified a method of applying 92 bis which may save, per witness, a third or half of the time even that that witness would take were he examined in full in the conventional way. We don't know how it's going to work out. We'll probably have our first 92 bis witnesses in the middle or end of next week. I hope so, certainly. But amongst other things that we should bear in mind, perhaps, is that by the use of that method of 92 bis, which may be applicable to even more witnesses than had been the subject of our application, we'll be able to save a great deal of time. For although I know, and well remember, the observations made from the Bench about the desirability of having critical bits of evidence given in detail in chief, sympathise with that, this is a trial which has difficulties of scale that have to be grappled with. And if one can save, with a large number of witnesses, a third of the time or half the time they would take by having them formally adopt their statement in front of an officer of the Chamber and then just giving cross-examination, well, we will have achieved much. The only additional observation I'd make in relation to 92 bis at this stage is this: If 92 bis witnesses, either in this sector of the trial or in any other sectors of the trial, are to give evidence but to be subject to cross-examination, we would ask consideration in due course to be given to so varying the provisions that they can come to the Tribunal on a single occasion, at the beginning stage of which they adopt and make whatever amendments that are necessary to their statement in front of an officer of the Chamber, and are then thereafter, a day or so later, giving evidence and being cross-examined. Because this would, of course, save an enormous amount of time, money, and administrative difficulty which follows from having the 92 bis formalities dealt with in the field. But that's another matter of detail, but it's something I would ask you to have in mind, if not immediately, then in due course. Because, of course, as we all know, for the taking of 92 bis statements, great teams of people, not just from the OTP but from the Registry, also have to go down to the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just two or three questions on the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Since you intend to use it as a particular approach to be followed in other binders, it will be useful to clarify some matters. In two or three cases, you seek to put in documentary evidence from persons whom you intend to call as witnesses. So the question is whether you wouldn't wait until those persons come as witnesses and have them -- have the documentary evidence put in through them. There were three cases like that. Also, there was a reference to Rule 70 materials. Rule 70 deals with matters not subject to disclosure. But when I looked, I didn't see any documents, so I didn't have any basis for making any determination or giving any advice to my colleagues on that matter. There are some pre-conflict victim photographs, and I wasn't able to understand the value of that, the pre-conflict victim photographs. And in relation to the British forensic team exhumation report, a general comment would be that it would seem to me that the presentation would be improved and rendered more intelligible by a system that identified the deceased persons listed in the schedule to the indictment, with the specifically named persons in the schedule of identification. But this may not be a matter of controversy, but perhaps it could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with those four points in reverse order, I entirely agree with the last point and I'm sure it's something that we should attend to. Dealing with the penultimate point, which I think was about the photographs of the deceased in life, yes, it is the case that such evidence is sometimes given by witnesses. Its relevance is more human than forensic. We have a duty not to overlook entirely the human interest in the case, but we are sparing in the way we present material that would have such an impact. The -- I think I may have missed the second point. The first point about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have that second point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first point was about documents, and I think Your Honour probably has in mind one or two hand-drawn maps. Unless the document is likely to be in any sense prejudicial, in the event of its not being proven, I would invite the Chamber to consider leaving such material in because frequently it's explanatory of something that is otherwise unclear in the statement. And again you can imagine the circumstance where you might have two different witnesses whose accounts would appear to match in writing but then the diligent amici or the accused would say, "But in fact you've only got to look at their plans or the other documents they produce to see that what they're saying is entirely at odds one with the other." So we would respectfully invite you to say that the statements together with produced documents should ordinarily go together. Now, Your Honour, that -- I don't know if that deals with Your Honour's questions. I'm sorry. Rule 70. As to that, such material will be provided as soon as it is possible for us to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could deal briefly, although it's coming up to 1.00, perhaps go on for another five minutes and give us a broad overview, because that is the matter we are most concerned with, I have to tell you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The statistics, which are raw statistics and which have been produced without my detailed participation because I've had to be involved in Court - I'm not suggesting they're not better for that; they're probably much better for my not being involved in this - but I'll hand them in in any event if I may, if the usher would be so good, are initially alarming, and then I'll hope to satisfy the Chamber that things are not alarming. To explain what's been done, each team was invited to, in the light of the way things have developed, to abandon any rule of thumb that says one witness per location or one witness per municipality, and say what would you actually -- what do we need in respect of any particular location to prove the case properly? So that if we start with Kosovo at the top, where in fact globally there's been comparatively little change, and the columns are divided as between X, those who have already been called, and Y, those to come, the -- and we perhaps needn't worry too much about anything other than crime base at the moment because -- for reasons that I can come to, but crime base, the total of 97 crime-base witnesses is what's presently identified, 17 already called, 80 to come, and that includes those who by whatever means are 92 bis. Perhaps I should again say in relation to 92 bis, of course 92 bis allows for statements to be read or even to be taken as read without the witness being called, and we aren't suggesting that the Chamber may not in other circumstances in other parts of the case say that 92 bis can operate in that way so that the evidence can simply be presented in written form, but we're working at the moment on the basis that the Chamber may, if the accused maintains his attitude towards 92 bis statements, want witnesses to come and be available for cross-examination. We don't encourage that, but we work on that basis. So that adding up the live witnesses and 92 bis witnesses, there are 80 more of those to come in total in relation to Kosovo. And that takes account of the fact that there would be investigators summarising some or all of the particular scenes. The Chamber will have in mind what's said in the motion about Racak, which is, of course, a particularly significant scene even if it features little in the indictment. It's significant because of the part it plays in the history. And the Chamber will know that the accused has already made considerable reference to it in his opening. And it's a scene where quite a number of witnesses will have to be called. But still, if our invitations are acceptable to the Chamber, this is a number of witnesses -- this is the number of witnesses whose necessity could be reviewed by the Chamber on review of binders, one by one, as we approach the evidence of a particular location. Turning to Croatia. Croatia presents a difficulty in one sense that, unlike Bosnia and save for the Dokmanovic trial, has not been the subject of any evidence thus far, so there's no possibility of saying in respect of any witness called and cross-examined on another occasion so we could put in a transcript. So again, the total --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Save for Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Save for Dokmanovic, yes, but not much of that would, I think, necessarily help. So that here are 126 crime-base witnesses. And what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff and her team have done for the purposes of 92 bis is simply to identify such witnesses as they feel can be taken in a shorter form under 92 bis. But this is a very rough-and-ready approach, not least because there may be different ways in which 92 bis may operate depending in part on the response of the accused to crime-base material, crime-base evidence in the other sectors of the trial. Bosnia is, of course, the case that raises the largest concern, but I've already indicated how it may be very significantly reduced. But thus far, looking at the 47 municipalities, a very large number of witnesses, 566 to cover crime base, are identified, or a large number. Incidentally, I better add again, parenthetically, although the figures are high, we don't suggest that if you're looking at three wars over the periods of time with which we are concerned, the overall number of sources is anything like extravagant, but it's a question of recognising the needs of a trial and all the other competing interests that operate here. Now, Mr. Groome and his team, on dividing up between viva voce and 92 bis, have had two things in mind in order to identify the witnesses who might be taken in shorter form. One, the witnesses that had already given evidence in other proceedings; and two, witnesses who appear to them at the review that it's possible to do in the time available, to be merely duplicative or confirmatory of other evidence. But now Bosnia - and I don't know if you want me to go on now beyond the five minutes you allowed me - needs a little more explanation, I think, as to where we are likely to be and why we are where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. 2.35. But, Mr. Nice, may I make it plain that we have obviously been considering matters during the break, and what we have in mind and what we wish you to address us on is this: We have in mind making an overall order for the length of the Prosecution case. We think this case must be brought under some broad direction, and everybody should know where we're going, and it might be helpful if we made an order in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I look -- can I deal with that after the break? Because it's something about which I want to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have an hour, and we must deal with the other outstanding issue about the Defence facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Can I correct a couple of things that I said this morning and amplify them, very briefly? I think I said in the Krstic case it was the witness Butler. Although I think the witness Butler may have referred to some witness statements, in fact, it was the witness Jean-Rene Ruez, the first witness in the case, whose evidence I had in mind, which indeed I've had printed out and which contains a quantity of summarising evidence of witnesses. I think Your Honour may have mentioned the possibility that summarising evidence was given in the case of Kvocka, and it was in relation to mass grave -- or a mass grave or mass graves. And odd that I should have overlooked this one, particularly of potential significance in relation to Bosnia. In Jelisic, at trial, the chief of investigations, John Ralston, gave extensive background evidence for the purposes of really establishing widespread and systematic conduct, built on witness evidence of which he was familiar but which wasn't given. So that that's one correction and some additions. Alert as I am to the time restraints here today, can I, in looking at the figures that we presented shortly before lunch, and before coming to Your Honour's question about an overall time for the case, draw something to your attention which I hope will be helpful? The Kosovo figures are broadly much as they had always been, save for the fact that witnesses we had thought might - in numbers, in any event - save for the fact that witnesses we had thought might be given 92 bis without being called at all will now have to be cross-examined, but the numbers are broadly the same. As a matter of history, in Kosovo, there were at least probably ten witnesses per site initially, reduced to five, and then the five further reduced, and thus to produce the figure. And of course, our invitation is that provided the Chamber is seized, in one way or another, of what the material amounts to overall, we can satisfy our responsibilities with this number of witnesses. Coming to Croatia, with the problems -- not the problems, the particular features of the history of this evidence that may affect us. In Croatia, there are 20 murder scenes, there are 17 detention camps, 3 deportation sites, and then there's Vukovar and Dubrovnik. So that without doing the math publicly, that's something in the region of only three witnesses per site. It's a very economic allocation at the moment, as we hope you will accept. Coming to Bosnia, at the moment, 47 municipalities, and I said I'd say a word about the history. At the time that the indictment or the -- yes, the indictment was proffered, the Prosecutor, who of course would have to be involved in any decision to change the indictment, had in mind - and I wasn't here at the time that this was effectively decided - had in mind the need to be consistent with other indictments that had already been served, and therefore if the 47 municipalities had been covered in the relevant associated indictments, there would have been no logic in pursuing a different course. Two things: First, there has already been some reduction in allegations made in the other indictments, so the consistency will enable a slight variation in Bosnia. Second, as I've explained in the motion -- and I hope I'm not going too fast. If I am, I'll slow down. As I've explained in the motion, there are, in the mind of the OTP generally, further radical proposals in relation to the Bosnian Serb cases which may enable further streamlining of those cases and thus of this. That's for your information, and I hope by way of encouragement, but nevertheless, that's a reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, sorry to interrupt you. You have mentioned several strategies for streamlining and reducing the case, but it occurs to me that there is one basic measure that the Prosecution could take and which it has not taken and that is just simply to reduce the size of the Prosecution case. So that instead of presenting evidence in respect of 47 municipalities, you would take what would be a representative sample, representative of the crimes charged in the indictment as a whole. Now, I say that because in the three years and three months I've been here, it's become quite clear to me that the prosecution of the most serious breaches of international humanitarian law cannot take place if there is brought to court and if there is sought to be presented in court evidence from every municipality or every crime site or every incident that is mentioned in the indictment. You may indict it, but I think serious consideration will have to be given by this Tribunal as to what is to be presented in court as evidence. If you have 47 municipalities, the question is: Why do you need to present evidence from the 47? Why can't you present evidence from a half of that or a third of that? And if you started in that way, instead of six seventy-eight witnesses for Bosnia and you were to take a third of the municipalities, you will probably have - I don't know - a third of that number. But that is really the problem that we have to grapple with. And until we can grapple with it, I think the Tribunal will always be facing a very serious problem. And under the international scrutiny as it is, I think it is going to be increasingly difficult for the Tribunal to devise strategies that will bring its work to an end. And I raise this as a matter for consideration, and perhaps it may have to be taken up at a different level, on an institutional basis, that the size of the Prosecution case, for the purposes of presentation of evidence, should be different, should be less than what is indicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm happy to say I'm in complete agreement with everything you've said, and indeed had already indicated this morning that plans are under way for the consideration of, for example, calling to the level of proof sufficient to make findings of fact sufficient to found convictions only perhaps half of these at this stage. These matters will, of course, have to be considered within the Office of the Prosecutor at its highest level, when I'm in a position to have those discussions, which I'm not, for example, this week, but that matter is under active consideration. And the Court will remember that I suggested this morning, perhaps much the way that it was dealt with in Jelisic, that to avoid allegations of cherry picking, these allegations having been raised in the indictment, it would be appropriate to proceed on the basis of a selection provided by whatever mechanism involving, for example, the amici as well, it would be possible to satisfy ourselves that the other material which might have no evidential weight, that the other material would not reveal anything inconsistent with what we were laying before you. Therefore, that does bring me to the potentially good news about Bosnia, because Bosnia is 49 -- 47 municipalities and a total of 566 crime-base witnesses, looking at the crime base. That's about 11 per municipality. Of course, some much larger, some much smaller. And the Court will remember that I told you that we started with Kosovo with about 10 per municipality and have gone through the process of being able to pare it down. Now, I'm not saying that we're necessarily going to be able to do that exercise to that degree because Bosnia is a bigger case. But bearing in mind that the accused's reaction to the crime-base evidence may be different, bearing in mind in particular that the Trial Chamber may be able to elicit from the accused, who doesn't negotiate with us directly at all, identification of issues which will enable perhaps witnesses to be given 92 bis without being called for cross-examination, if his contest there is different from here and so on, there is, I think, every reason to believe by the time we have been in a position or are in a position to announce our much narrower focus in terms of municipalities, 25 or Your Honour might wish it to be less and it may be possible to be less, but if we start with 25, this case can become, I'm quite sure, manageable. And that brings me to the question that His Honour Judge May asked me immediately before the break about the length of the case. I must respectfully decline to give an overall length of time for two reasons, really. One, I simply can't at the moment; and two, I having experience that shows that it may be undesirable, certainly at this stage of any trial, to fix a time limit, because of course that makes ultimately the Prosecution vulnerable to the length of cross-examination which can serve the purpose, as it may have done in an earlier case intentionally otherwise, of consuming time and thus shutting out evidence. And it's our respectful submission that what's important is that this case should be managed so as to identify the issues and bring the necessary evidence to deal with the issues but no more than that in showing that the Chamber is adequately seized of all the material it needs to be seized of. And against the notion of setting a time limit on a case at this stage, I am fortified by a decision of the Appeals Chamber in Galic. And it's dated the 14th of December. And in that case a time limit was imposed -- I'm sorry. I've only just very helpfully been reminded of the decision by Mr. Groome, and I haven't got copies for you. I can make mine available, of course, immediately. And a particular time limit of 380 -- 280 hours was set. And His Honour Judge Hunt, who presided, made this observation in paragraph 7, taking it very shortly, having dealt with the powers under 73 bis and (E) and said: "Unfortunately as the brief description of the Pre-Trial Conference demonstrates, it was anything but clear what the final issues in dispute were to be at the time when the Trial Chamber imposed the restriction upon the length of the Prosecution case. The Trial Chamber's discretion in fixing that restriction therefore miscarried and error has been established." Now, here I ask the Chamber to accept that everything that all parts of the OTP in all three indictments it has done so far has shown that it has no desire to extend this case. On the contrary, it has the desire to do everything it can to keep things as short as they properly can. It's certainly my personal desire, as I'm sure it is everybody else's. Nobody wants to extend the case unnecessarily by one day. But issues aren't yet identified and they can't be, but the time will come when they can be. And my invitation to the Chamber is, as I set out in the motion that the Chamber and the Prosecution, without in any sense working together other than publicly and in court, can to some degree work together to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will probably not be. At some stage, in the way this case goes, the middle of the Bosnian hearing that the issues will become clear, if then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's possible it would be as late as that, but, Your Honour, it's also possible that there will be a sufficient identity of approach in Croatia and Bosnia that it will be earlier than that. But in any event, if we make it plain by our conduct of the Kosovo case that we're not in any sense doing other than move things along as swiftly as possible, and we have the assistance of the Chamber, where appropriate, in clarifying issues with the accused to enable that to happen, and if the Chamber is minded to accept any of the proposals I've made as to abbreviating time, then although we won't know when the trial will end, we will know that it's being dealt with timeously, and that should be enough, because simply to impose an overall time limit at this stage would be to do something that has an element of arbitrariness about it, which might be undesirable and unfair. So that if I return to the statistics, which I say are very rough --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the statistics show - and this is why we have in mind the time limit - the proposal to call over a thousand witnesses. No trial can take place in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I know you say that it's merely a list and nothing more, but the fact is that there are over a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I hope I made it plain, it's not my proposal that we should call these. This is a list that shows what witnesses would be required were we to prove all aspects of the case in the entirely conventional way, with every witness coming to Court. We have no expectation or intention of doing that. There is already the substantial reduction from the Bosnian part, and we are confident that arrangements can be made in accordance with the Tribunal's rules and regulations to take some of these witnesses in different methods and some of them not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In the case of Bosnia, there has been a great deal of litigation; less so, of course, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But in the case of Bosnia, there's been a great deal of litigation covering many of the issues which you'll be seeking to cover. It would seem to me that you could cover a lot of that by use of transcript evidence and the like --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and thus shorten the matter. It may be that the crucial issue in this case is going to be the connection between the accused and these allegations, and it may be that, certainly in the case of Bosnia and Croatia, that those are the matters which concentration should be centred on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We hope that will be the position, and that's why I've been saying throughout that the accused's reaction to Bosnia crime-base evidence may be entirely different from his reaction to Kosovo evidence, where NATO and the insurgency, if it was, of the KLA features in his questioning. So I've simply listed -- this is not a list of witnesses to be called, and we are doing everything we can to take matters shortly. I should say also, Your Honour, that the question of taking judicial notice of findings in other trials is a project that is under active consideration and applies particularly again in relation to Bosnia. So all these mechanisms are in mind and in development. But without a represented accused, we have to initially prepare on the basis that we may have to prove anything and everything, and we hope that by cooperation with the amici and with the assistance, if appropriate and where appropriate, of the Chamber, we will actually be able to bring each of these trials to a proper and safe conclusion within the minimum time that the issues identified by the accused will demand. But we very respectfully suggest that fixing a time limit now would not be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have, during the time which this case has been adjourned over the last three weeks, had occasion to consider the overall conduct of it. It is a case of immense scope and also a case, of course, of great importance. We are charged with the management of it, and during the adjournment we have been considering what is reasonable, in the light of the Statute, for us to order in terms of trial management. Such management is necessary in order that the trial can be brought to an end within a reasonable time. Our duty also under the Statute is to ensure that the trial is fair and expeditious and is conducted with due regard to the rights of the accused and also having in mind the interests of the victims and witnesses. All these are matters which we've had to consider. The interests of justice and the fairness of the trial means, of course, fairness to both sides. It does not mean purely fairness to the accused or to the Prosecution, but to both sides. And we've had to balance these various issues, and the conclusion we've come to is that it is necessary, in order that this trial is conducted in an expeditious fashion, to fix a date for the close of the Prosecution case. We can only do that in order to concentrate minds and to ensure that the matter is completed fairly. A trial has also to be conducted with this in mind: that an accused, whether he is represented or not, must be in a position to defend himself against the charges against him, and the longer the Prosecution case goes on, it may be said, the more difficult it is and the more onerous it is for the accused to do so. And in order to ensure a fair trial, we must make sure that an accused is in the position, reasonably, to defend himself against the various charges. We also have to bear in mind that at the end of a trial, the Trial Chamber has to give a judgement. The longer the trial goes on, the more difficult that is, and if it stretches into a matter of years, it, of course, becomes more difficult still. These are the matters we have in mind. I should say that we also have in mind that of course it's the duty of the Prosecution to put forward their case, and they must be given reasonable opportunity to do so, and it's not for the Trial Chamber to try and dictate in any arbitrary way how the Prosecution go about proving their case. It's a matter for them to do. But nonetheless, we have decided that, in the interests of justice, we must fix a date. We've heard the submissions of the Prosecution today, and of course we bear them in mind and we will consider ways in which evidence can be put properly before the Trial Chamber, and expeditiously. But nonetheless, we do not consider it inappropriate to fix a date at this time. We, of course, pay attention to what was said in Galic, but with respect, the decision in this case has to be made at this stage. It may well be that the issues will never be plain until the beginning of the Defence case in the particular circumstances of this case. With all this in mind, we have decided that the Prosecution should have one year from today to conclude their case. That will give them a total of 14 months in which to finish the case, their case. In the view of the Trial Chamber, no Prosecution case should continue for a period longer than that. I would add this: that of course it is our duty to ensure that the cross-examination is continued within reasonable limits. We shall do that. We shall ensure that unreasonable amount of time is not wasted in cross-examination. At this stage, we shall not seek to come to any conclusions about the number of witnesses that should be called. It's a matter for the Prosecution. But during the course of discussion, ways in which the scope of this case can properly be brought within a proper range have been suggested, and there are ways which can be pursued. As far as the timetable is concerned, the recesses are known. We will, in fact, adjust slightly the Christmas recess. This part of the indictment should finish, it's to be hoped, within a reasonable time before the recess so that there is time before the next part, but it may be that we can address that conduct in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Two things: As to the recess, the summer recess, I've set out in a motion how common witnesses, witnesses common to two parts of the trial, could either come at the end of Kosovo or at the beginning of the next section. I gather that the recess is indeed only three weeks in the summer and there's going to be no extended period made available between parts of the case for preparation of the next sector in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we can finish this part, there will be additional time in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but if we can't, there will only be the three weeks; there won't be an extended period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have to see, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not asking for one, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but the date -- how the time between now and next year is arranged, of course, will have to be considered in due course, but it's the final date that we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Obviously, we'll work to that. But as to the recess, what I was going to say is that if we reach the stage by then of the witnesses common to two parts, we will simply, if this is satisfactory, use common witnesses up until the end of the period before the recess and then start with common witnesses afterwards, because they provide a useful bridge for parts of the case in any event. The second thing that I would ask, I hope not impertinently, is this: We have the recesses for the summer and for Christmas, next Christmas. The length of the days I'm not sure are necessarily known to us at the moment. Where a Prosecution is under a strict timetable, as this would be, changing the daily timetable, especially if it was reduction of hours, could affect us, in the same way as ill health could affect us. And although I'm not looking forward to any such interruptions Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. - on the contrary, I hope they wouldn't occur - may it be that there could, if appropriate, be extension to take account of that sort of unforeseen event or are they to be built in as an incident of the timetable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us work on the basis that they're built in, but clearly there are matters which may need consideration in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will go from there to consider the Defence facilities. Mr. Milosevic, I'm just going to ask the amicus for something about their brief and then it will be your turn. Yes, or indeed any other matters, Mr. Wladimiroff, that you want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have only a few observations related to the facilities. Let me start to say that we have seen in the report of the Registrar that the Registrar has taken some pre-observations dealing with the matter before listing out what their views are on each of the facilities we have listed in our brief. Let me deal with these pre-observations very shortly. If you have got it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have the Registrar's proposals or propositions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 8 and 9 and further on on page 10, you will find three observations by the Registrar claiming that the rights of the accused cannot be unrestricted but restricted by the interest of justice, and on page 9, be subject to the interest of an effectively conducted trial, and thirdly, on page 10, restrictions may be based upon legitimate interest of security. We do understand these observations, but it seems to us that it follows from Article 20 of the Statute that the rights of the accused can only be restricted as far as required in our Article 22 by the interest of witnesses and -- yes, by witnesses. So therefore, we believe that if we talk about the rights of the accused and the facilities related to that, it's more or less a matter how to structure his rights in relation to the needs of his defence and not a matter of being restricted by any other observations or any other interest. Now, you may have noticed that we listed in our brief a number of facilities, on page 4 and 5, and if I may go through the list of the Registrar dealing with our list, I've got a few observations. First of all, as far as the facilities are concerned in the Detention Unit, we take it that by the word "mail," the Registrar is also including e-mail, more specifically is referring to e-mail. The Registrar makes an observation saying that there will be no facility for mails or fax during the weekends. We suggest that that is a matter for consideration, that the accused should also have that facility during the weekends, taking into account that most working days he is in court. So that would cripple him for the Mondays if he had no opportunity to use these facilities the days before the first working day of the next week. Next one, telephone. We are satisfied by the observations of the Registrar, though we suggest that the time restraint which can be expanded on request of the accused from 6.00 up to 8.00 should also be allowed during the weekends and, even better, perhaps to 10.00 in the evenings. As far as visits are concerned, that seems satisfactory as well except for the restriction on the weekends. It does not make sense to us that there is a full restriction for the weekends for those who are assisting Mr. Milosevic and that according to rules as explained by the Registrar, the weekends are only available to family members or friends. I think it's a matter for the accused to decide what he prefers, people to visit him on the weekends to be family members or those who help him out in his case. It's not matter for the Registrar, we feel. So that's a matter for consideration as well. The time limit for visits in the detention centre is 16.45. So that seems not to be relevant for working days, or it may be extended for legal advisors to 8.00 in the evening. We suggest that should be extended to 9.00 in the evenings. As far as photocopying facilities, it seems satisfactory what has been observed by the Registrar, though it is limited to 8.00 -- sorry, to 6.00. Keeping in mind that he will return after 6.00, it seems reasonable to extend that time limit to 10.00 in the evening. Last but not least, the VCR facilities, which are fine, and the laptop facilities, which we feel is also quite sufficient. Then dealing with the facilities in court, the telephone facilities, if available -- we heard the accused about it not being available all day, but I take it that if that was an incident that telephone facilities are available and working on all days, that's fine for us. There's only one issue here. He is allowed to make telephone calls during the breaks and before the hearings, not after. It seems to me it's either to extend the facility of having access to the telephone in the Detention Unit or to extend it here. It's either in the court or there, but he should have a proper opportunity to evaluate what happens that day with the purpose to prepare for the next day. If I now speak about the fax facility. That seems reasonable to us. We have no comment here. And that goes also for photocopying. The Registrar is pointing out that the photocopying should only be allowed on an exceptional basis. We feel that is not right. It should be where needed, and that is, I think, a better test than to review whether there's an exception or not. Now, after having dealt with that, I think I should also say something about the propositions for further defence facilities. We are satisfied with these proposals. It seems fair enough to have two persons who are qualified, as set out by the Registrar, to assist the accused on a more regular basis. Again, here I stress that if these facilities are limited to communications during working days and not during the weekends, that might be an unnecessary handicap. So I draw your attention again to my observations in terms of time limits and day limits. We are satisfied with the proposal that these advisors should -- should be persons who are within Rule 44, the requirements of Rule 44 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And we are also satisfied that these people are bound by the code of ethics. If I now deal with a more difficult issue, that is what the accused asked about the right to disclose materials to third parties or his associates, but before I do that perhaps I would stop here because that's more beyond the facilities that I have discussed so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have any general submissions before we hear from the accused about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. Let me then deal with that matter, Your Honour. It seems to us consistent to make a distinction between confidential materials and let me phrase it as "regular materials." If I'm right in thinking that regular materials, as I label them, are materials that are or shall be in the public domain, then it seems to us that there should not be any restriction on communications with the advisors of the accused in that area. So the issue is what to do with confidential matters. It seems to us if the advisors are those who fall within the restrictions of Rule 44 and they are bound by the code of ethics, it seems all right to us that the accused will be allowed under these conditions to communicate with his assistants to enable the assistants to do what they should do, that is, to assist him also in these matters. So far, there is no evidence known to the amici that shows that such kind of communications would be asking for trouble, so to say. We have heard a lot in this courtroom about events that are or may sound troublesome, but at the end of the day, the amici, reviewing that, did not find any evidence that that is for the accused to blame. So we believe there is no precedent here to limit him in any way as long as he is communicating with these advisors who fall under Rule 44 and who are known by name, as set out in the proposal of the Registrar. The consequence of it would be that your rulings on witness protection need not to be changed because it's already within your orders that such communications aren't forbidden as long as they're not with those who are within the rules, that is, appointed advisors by name who act as an advisor though not as an attorney in court, because they are under Rule 44 and therefore bound by the code and the Rules. So we believe that would be a workable basis. From there, we advise the Court to follow that pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, before you make your general submissions, your request, as we understand it, is that witness statements, summaries, and other materials, including exhibits, be handed to associates of yours in order that you can prepare your defence. Now, you can perhaps clarify that. And you've heard what the amicus has suggested as a way forward dealing with confidential materials, and also at the suggestion of the Registry that it may be possible to make an order along those lines, although there is a problem, as you'll appreciate, with the confidential material. Now, would you like to address us on that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be given an opportunity first to comment on the one-and-a-half-hour-long speech of the opposite party before I say anything about this other issue that you have raised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We made a ruling on that, but you can make a comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not entering into whether you have made a ruling or not. You are doing what you will anyway. But I think that for the benefit of the public, it is necessary for me to comment on what we have heard from the other side. First of all, I underlined several times here, and I wish to do it once again, that what was set out at the beginning as to me allegedly participating in the proceedings is not true, because I do not recognise this Tribunal. And I have said several times that I will avail myself of every opportunity to speak in the interest of the truth, and I do so regardless of whether it is an opportunity you are giving me, when the time for the cross-examination comes, or on occasions such as this one when you're giving me a chance to make a comment. But generally speaking, all that we've heard over the hour and a half has only one single value to it, and that is that the public as a whole and professionals in the public will be able to learn about an innovative recipe as to how to push forward a false indictment at all costs, how to pretend, to set up a fake trial and to organise a trial without a trial, to make something more nonsensical than it already is. Namely, I understand what we have heard as an effort for one side working for the other side what it considers to be in the interest of the other side but also to take upon itself the competencies of the Trial Chamber. I'm not surprised that they wish to do that, because this false Prosecution must try and reduce the fiasco of the false witnesses they are producing, and that is why, among others, instead of witnesses, we have lately been hearing certain quasi-scientific reports. I think it is absolutely unacceptable that they should request that any binders of theirs should have any value. They could not have any such value before any legal tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should have said that you're entitled to address us on the binders since we're considering the admissibility. So if you want to address us on that, do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, this question of so-called comprehensive witnesses or overlapping witnesses and using investigators working for the Prosecution as witnesses is nonsense, because it emerges that the investigators who are working for the OTP are placed in the position of judges to assess what is relevant and what is not relevant in the witness statements. And then this question of summaries of witness statements, which is being encouraged only because in summaries it is possible to delete everything that stands in the way of the other side for the cross-examination, and we have already seen many examples of contradictions between the prior statements given by witnesses and their statements here and the cross-examination. So this is an offensive of that side over there to belittle and make up for the obvious problems they are confronted with. How can an investigator be a witness? If somebody is working for one party, they can provide the results of their work to that party, and that party cannot use them as a witness when he was not there. He has nothing to testify about.
