He only can interpret what is written in the indictment only in different words based on alleged statements that he heard from those who allegedly took part and were present when something occurred. I think that this is to such a degree an absurd idea that no normal or legitimate court would accept it. They even mentioned, for instance - let me just use an example - that forensic reports can be provided without identifying the victims. What do such reports mean unless the victims are identified? I can understand if, for instance, one were to identify all the terrorists that were killed in Racak and we were to establish that they were not inhabitants of Racak but terrorists coming from other places, and so on, but I don't think that any legal court could accept that. So I'm saying this not because I insist on you accepting something or not, because that is up to you, and this is illegal anyway; I'm just drawing attention to the absurdness of the requests made here, unfortunately in public. So the gist of it, the contents of the false indictment and false witnesses, should be exposed to the public as little as possible, because in that case, it will be less exposed to verification of the truth, and then, on that basis, all kinds of fabrications can be produced. So what is being suggested is actually the use of propaganda methods, to pack elements and so-called witnesses in the way that media reports are written. They say somebody said something, somebody else something else, such-and-such thing happened. This is all packaged up: This happened, and here you are. All you have to do is accept it. So a way is being looked for for these witnesses who have proven to be vulnerable, to be made unvulnerable [sic], to be reduced to summaries, and instead of them, certain investigators to be put forward, for the investigators to judge, as if they were judges, what is relevant and what is irrelevant, and then to build this whole tower of cards on the basis of these so-called comprehensive witnesses. So I think those who are working for the OTP cannot represent their information as testimony. They can only produce their findings to those for whom they work, and it is up to them to make the selection. So I think for a regular court, no witness that does not appear in person can be taken into consideration, and a witness who does appear to testify must have his complete original statement to be used as a basis for the cross-examination and he must appear in court. Secondly, I know that you have made a ruling before, and I'm not questioning that. That is up to you anyway. You have already made a ruling about Rule 92 bis that the Prosecution is returning to again in the same way that it discussed it before you made your ruling. So I think that this is highly transparent, I would say, in the justification of saving time and money, but in fact, to make construction as to assert a false indictment, and to make invulnerable vulnerable witnesses, and to fake a Tribunal and a trial. As for this second matter, it can be reduced to several points, this matter that Mr. Wladimiroff spoke about. First of all, you put on the agenda, as far as I know, the facilities for the accused - that is, myself - with respect to defence, and those facilities are next to none. Allow me to say again: I'm not asking you for anything. I am just noting, for the benefit of the public, that the right to defence, which you yourself have proclaimed, is, on the other hand, by your conduct, physically made impossible. Today is I don't know what date. The 10th of April, I assume. So two months ago the trial started, and I still cannot communicate with my associates. Here is Mr. Tomanovic sitting behind the glass partition here. In the last few weeks he has been able to visit me for 45 minutes, and in the presence of representatives of the Tribunal. That is all the possibilities I have in terms of communication with my associates, that I have had so far. Therefore, it would be logical, even though it is a tactic to keep me isolated, that is, for the OTP to engage in the machinations I have just described, and despite that, I am kept in total isolation. Obviously, this cannot be remedied by cosmetic measures such as are being offered, but it would be logical for me to be able to freely communicate with my associates, to be able to freely communicate in terms of telephone, faxes, et cetera, and also to have the necessary time to do that. Because you can say that I have the right to I don't know how many associates - one hundred - but if you don't give me the necessary time to see them, they are of no use to me, because it is physically not possible to see them nor to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The associates -- two of the associates are the gentleman you mentioned, Mr. Tomanovic, and Mr. Ognjanovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are my associates, which are present here and with whom I do communicate. You asked me: What about the documents? As things stand now -- because somebody has to get information for me about your witnesses, whose statements I am given, because I certainly don't have that information at hand. So now I am being told that these original witness statements, I have to read them to them on the telephone, on a public call phone in the Detention Unit corridor, for them to prepare some information for me relative to those witnesses, and then for them to find some sort of way of passing on to me that information. For instance, some information that was sent to me on Friday I couldn't receive before Monday because there was no one there. Either it's being checked out or reviewed or supervised, et cetera. So for me, it is plain that if I have associates, they need to be able to communicate with me in the breaks, in the Detention Unit, for them to get the documents that are given to me so that I don't have to call them on the phone and dictate them to them, but that they can pick them up directly when collecting information and data about them. Then, in the course of cross-examination, how do you imagine cross-examination to go on from 9.00 to 5.00 and then for me to meet with my associates, to collect information, to read what is given to me, to review it during the night, and then to start working again at 9.00 a.m.? So if you don't give me the time, half the working day, then that is nowhere near the principle of the equality of arms. Because the two sides here are supposed to be exchanging arguments. Then both sides have time to prepare, rather than one side having a hundred per cent of the time and the other side none at all. So that the question of time and the working hours during the day that the other side is suggesting, with absolutely inappropriate allusions as to conditions of health, I think is a factor of great significance as to the facilities given or not. Therefore, the question of communications, associates, and time, all these are things that each of you are able to organise according to your own criteria, including sleeping, feeding, and all other vital needs, like taking some fresh air, and so on. So as not to take up any more time - I don't need several hours, as the other side seems to need - I'm not asking for anything. I simply wish to underline that your proclaimed right to defence, which you have constituted as a right, has absolutely been -- I have been absolutely deprived of it by physical means. And that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, anybody who has heard you cross-examine would realise that you've been in receipt of material. But we'll consider your application and we'll make a ruling on it. Mr. Kay or Mr. Wladimiroff, I haven't given you the opportunity to address us on the binders. I don't know if you have any submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We were waiting for that. The accused's position on this matter is plainly clear from the argument that he's just presented to the Court. One of the problems that seemed to us to be apparent from this is: It's very difficult for anyone listening to the Prosecution to be aware quite what weight the Trial Chamber should give to such evidence. It seemed that it wasn't being used to prove offences, it wasn't being used to the fullest extent that evidence is sought to be produced in Court, but was to be used as background evidence that the Prosecutor was saying would be helpful to the Trial Chamber. That may well be the case, but it's very unclear then as to the rights of the accused against such background evidence, and it's very unclear to us as to how, on the Prosecution's argument, the Court itself should apply that evidence and what standards should be applied. We appreciate that this is part of their proposal to speed up proceedings and to put the full extent of their case, as they say it is, before the Court, but this is not material that's been taken in an investigative system under juge d'instruction or similar judicial control by the Trial Chamber itself. It's merely outside that. It's the evidence of investigators who have spoken to witnesses, who thereby report what those witnesses have said, without any examination of the background of the witnesses or of the incidents themselves. In those circumstances, again, it's very difficult to know what exactly the Trial Chamber should make of it. This is a case perhaps that needs to have more focus on the indictment itself rather than seeking to go down every alleyway and byway of Kosovo and elsewhere in Yugoslavia. One is very conscious of the allegations within the indictment, and that's where the focus of the case should be, to be fair to the accused himself. He should perhaps be hearing more evidence based upon the indictment that's been brought against him and the issues concerning his responsibility rather than these other issues. It seems to us that the Prosecution are looking at incidents rather than perhaps focusing on events and thereafter transferring their attention to the indictment itself. The binders, in many respects, highlight this problem, because at the end of the day, if the binder goes in to the extent that the Prosecutor wants, it may be from their perspective a full analysis of what happened, but in a way, perhaps such a detailed analysis is not needed in relation to the indictment against this accused, and all it does is occupy his time in having to deal with those issues that are not meaningful to him. And we can see, as we all know, that time is of concern to all the parties within this case. The Trial Chamber has imposed a time limit today, quite how, in the Prosecution structure or timetable that they put before the Trial Chamber today, how much time would be taken up by those crime-base witnesses recording particular and specific incidents or events. So in relation to the binders, we follow what the accused has put before the Court, but if the Court is to go down any route that would enable them to be accepted as evidence before the Court, it's difficult to see how it can be separated in some form from background to not becoming evidence, that the Trial Chamber has to express precisely what is meant by the use of that material so that those dealing with it will be aware of the risk and issues at stake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Things like the exhumation report, and reports and documents of that kind, photographs, all that sort of thing, we've tended to admit in the past as being in a rather different category to witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. One could see that material evidence, evidence that has been produced for the investigation, that reflects specific aspects of the investigation, photographs and whatsoever, may well be produced in that form, and has been produced in virtually all the cases before this Tribunal and the other Tribunal dealing with Rwanda. If issues arise concerning such photographs and such material that seeks to establish a particular point in relation to authenticity, veracity of the particular body or subject that's being photographed, that's an issue that can thereafter be opened up and there be an examination of it specifically before the Court on the evidence, and we would foresee that that is a way of dealing with issues such as that. But the main problem, and it seems to us the main problem that the accused would face, is of those reports to the investigators by other people, which are classically hearsay and may be third-, fourth-, fifth-hand hearsay in relation to some of the material that would thereby be produced. In many respects, the need for those witnesses is really open to question, but it's for the Prosecutor to consider the presentation of the case. It's their responsibility and it's for them to make the decisions relevant to that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Nice, we've really overrun our time. We were supposed to have adjourned at half past 3.00. But briefly, if you could respond on one particular issue, which is the handing over of the statements to associates. Is there anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, and a couple of sentences, if I may, in answer to Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Handing over to associates, unless qualified lawyers recognising the Tribunal, simply should not be allowed. We have to protect these witnesses. There is a perfectly full regime whereby the represented accused can have access to material that is otherwise highly confidential and exposes witnesses to very great risk. It is wholly unacceptable to the Office of the Prosecutor that its statements should be handed over other than in a controlled regime. We have to remind the Chamber of the various publications that have been made. I have one that I suspect is with the Registry or with the Chamber already, coming from the association that represents this accused out of Court, from Danas [phoen], of the 2nd of March. I'll hand it in again. In fact, information provided from a functionary of his political party, the SPS, although it doesn't say it in the short translation that accompanies it, where the unnamed official of the association says: "We know who the protected witnesses are. In the case of Albanian women who claimed they have been raped, we won't disclose any details because neither President Milosevic nor we wish to abuse their misfortune. When KLA commanders appear as witnesses, only then will we have a chance to show all that we have found out." It would be wholly wrong for any special provision to be made to the associates of this accused to accommodate the fact that he and they choose not to recognise this Tribunal. Provision in the ordinary course to people who have codes of conduct controlling their behaviour, yes; otherwise, in our respectful submission, definitely no. May I make two points in relation to what Mr. Kay said, because it's on the binder, and if I may be permitted. First, I don't quite understand what he says about the Prosecution not being focused. All the evidence that's been brought has been exactly on the crime-base matters that we have to prove. We don't have any choice in that. As to the value to be placed on material of a summarising nature, I've made my position clear, and for the avoidance of any doubt, I repeat: Its evidential value on the positive side would be slight, although I'm not suggesting it would be nonexistent. Its real value is elsewhere as a check and to avoid that most undesirable of outcomes, which could be that this Chamber's decisions could be criticised as a leap of faith from over-selective material to which the scale of the case would otherwise compel us. We simply are concerned that those criticisms can be avoided by the Chamber being properly seized of knowledge of all the material. Your Honour, I have a couple of other administrative matters of information to give. That's all. Can I do that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As long as it's quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One, we are submitting a motion for the extension of the limit of the pre-trial brief. This arises again from the desire to achieve uniformity with the other cases. We've gone, you may recall, for a hundred-page limit, I think, initially. The Plavsic/Krajisnik case, which is closely associated and for which there must be common elements, has made an application for a much longer brief, and I'm not minded to be compelled to the shorter form. If we are to have passages that are exactly common to both cases, we are making an application to extend, and I hope that will be understood in that history. Our general policy has always been for brevity, but it will be impossible to achieve parallel approaches if we're having to use entirely difference periods of time. Second, we are encountering difficulties as a result of resources here within the Tribunal generally, partly from budgetary matters and so on, with the provision of materials on the due date, the 30th of April. We are publishing a report on that, together with a proposal that this is a matter that might be dealt with by your legal officer on a continuing basis under 65 ter, whatever it is. But that report's coming your way. It's available at the moment but I shan't weary you at the moment. It's in the form of a memorandum that's going to come as a motion, unless you want to see it as a memorandum this afternoon, but those applications will be before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I think this is the last chance for me or the Chamber to clarify - not to you, Mr. Nice; it's to Mr. Milosevic - clarify the position of the accused. I understand that it is of your own decision not to be represented by counsel, and it was decided before I arrived here, but in my opinion, to recognise the Tribunal is one thing and to have counsel is another matter. I have heard that you have been speaking in the interest of truth, and why not having an attorney, or counsel, or legal advisor named by you in the interest of truth? Could you address it later on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you an answer straight away. Would you like me to give you an answer straight away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot appoint a lawyer, an attorney for myself, in front of an institution that I don't recognise. I think you are not a legitimate court, and you are well aware of that because you're all experts in international law. And the sole thing that this Tribunal has is the force of might, of those who appointed it, not international law or international right, domestic, continental, Anglo-Saxon, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I address the Court after the break on this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it will have to be before the break because we've got to hear another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. It's a very short one, Your Honours. Picking up what has been said, also in the view of the amici, there is a difference between a counsel and a counsel with the, let me phrase it, right of audience. In our view, it would be possible for the accused to appoint counsel who assists him in this case, that counsel being recognised by the Registrar as counsel under Article 44, though without instructions of the accused to represent him in court. Therefore, at least totally aside whether the accused recognises the court or not, it is irrelevant for counsel as well because he will not represent the accused in court. Some people might say, "I don't know whether that's a right description that the accused is waiving the right of his counsel to address the court," but effectively he is pointing to counsel it's a matter for him, not for the Court. The only matter for the Court is, at least for the Registry is, to accept or recognise that counsel. And as long as that counsel is not instructed by the accused to represent him in court, that could not be understood as an expression of the accused of recognition of the court, and the matter of the Registrar to recognise that counsel is not a matter that affects the accused's position of not recognising the Court. So in our view, it would be possible to have the accused and these two lawyers, who are lawyers under Rule 44, to be appointed by him, to be recognised by the Registrar. That would allow a communication between these two lawyers and the accused which is a client-privileged relation. That will solve a lot of issues. And these two lawyers are under the Rules of the Tribunal. They are subject to contempt of court and the code of ethics. As far as disciplinary matters, not yet under the Tribunal, under the Rules of the Tribunal, but under their domestic rules. One of the amici is well in the position to judge that, what would be appropriate if there was any breach. So in our view, it would be feasible as long as we did not, let's say, focus on the wrong issue and that is by his choice to appoint counsel and by recognition of that choice had nothing to do with recognition of the Tribunal. That's all I want to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The accused will have heard what you've said. We will adjourn now for as short a time as possible. I'll ask the Registrar how long it's going to take.
